The suitability conditions are
$c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{a}O\}\ge t+1\;\forall i\in O$ and
$d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\}\le u\;\forall j\notin O$, 
$\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$.  Hence a non empty $O$ with $|O|=k$ can only
exist for $n\ge k(t+1)$.  For $m=4$ the three interesting cardinalities
are $k=1,2,3$.

With $|O|=3$ the outside item is the number of first place votes of the
deleted item, $d_{j}(O)=f_{j}$, and $c_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$.  Put
$f_{(1)}\le f_{(2)}\le f_{(3)}\le f_{(4)}$, $\sum f_{i}=n$.
If $f_{(2)}>t$ we can delete the minimal first place item and obtain a
triple with $c_{i}(O)>t$ for the three remaining items and
$d(O)=f_{(1)}\le\lceil n/4\rceil$.
With the usual normalisation $n=4(t+1)=84$ this gives 
$d(O)=t+1$ and the regular $4$-cycle
$1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $2\succ3\succ4\succ1$, $3\succ4\succ1\succ2$,
$4\succ1\succ2\succ3$ with $t+1$ agents of each type shows the bound
$t+1=21$ is best possible for a triple.  That is the $t+1$ first place
form of the statement.

With $|O|=2$ let $\{i,j\}$ be a $t$–strong pair,
$c_{i},c_{j}\ge t+1$.  The two outside items can be written as
$r_{k}=d_{k}(\{i,j\})$.  Averaging over the six unordered pairs gives a
pair with $r_{k}+r_{\ell}\le 2(t+1)$ and in the $n$-free formulation
the worst case is $\max_{k\notin\{i,j\}}r_{k}\le2t$.  In the
strict $>t$ formulation this is usually quoted as
$u=2t+1=41$, i.e. $u_{*}=2t=40$ up to the customary $+1$.
The two-block profile $a\ge b$, $a+b=n$, shows
$\min_{O}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)\ge\lceil n/2\rceil$ for a pair and the
$2t$ bound is attained for $n=2(t+1)$.

The deletion argument is $n$–free.  Repeatedly delete an $i\in O_{k}$ with
$c_{i}(O_{k})\le t$.  After the deletions we obtain $O^{*}\neq\varnothing$
with $c_{i}(O^{*})>t$ for all $i\in O^{*}$ and
$d_{j}(O^{*})\le (m-|O^{*}|)t$ for every $j\notin O^{*}$.  Hence a
universal $n$–free guarantee is
\[
u_{0}(m,t)=(m-1)t,
\]
and for $m=4$, $t=20$ this is $u_{0}=3t=60$, $61$ in the strict
$<u$ formulation.  With the conventional normalisation $n=m(t+1)$ the
$3$–set can be taken and the sharp first place value is $t+1=21$,
often reported as the pair $2t=40$/$41$ bound
$u=2(t+1)=42$ in the literature.

The disagreement in the round is exactly the normalisation of $n$.
$21$ is the sharp first place value for the minimal feasible instance
$n=4(t+1)$; $40$–$41$, i.e. $2t$, is the usual pair core constant;
$60$ is the best $n$-free, i.e. $(m-1)t$, guarantee.  The $42=2(t+1)$
value is the same $2(t+1)$ averaging bound written in the $t+1$
convention.  No finite $u$ can be $n$-independent for truly
unbounded $n$, because for $|O|=1$, $\min_{i}\max_{j}w_{j,i}\ge n/2$,
so the problem is understood modulo the conventional $n=m(t+1)$,
$n=2(t+1)$ normalisations above.

The discussion is about the size of the set that can be forced to be
t-loaded and at the same time to have a small outside preference.  For a set
$O$,

$c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{a}O\}$, $\;\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$,
$d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\}$, $j\notin O$,

and $O$ is suitable iff $c_{i}(O)>t\;(i\in O)$ and $d_{j}(O)\le u\;(j\notin O)$.
In particular $k(t+1)\le n$ is necessary for $|O|=k$.

For $m=4$ the only $n$-free regimes are $|O|=1,2,3$.  With
$|O|=3$ and $O=[4]\setminus\{k\}$ we have $d_{k}(O)=f_{k}$ the first place
number of $k$ and $c_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}\;(i\in O)$.  Hence a triple can be made
$t$-loaded as soon as three items have $f_{i}>t$ and then

$d(O)=\min_{k}f_{k}\le \lceil n/4\rceil $.

On the usual normalisation $n=m(t+1)=4(t+1)$ the balanced $4$-cycle

$1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;
4\succ1\succ2\succ3$,

$21$ agents of each type for $t=20$, has $f_{i}=t+1$ for every $i$ and
$c_{i}([4]\setminus\{k\})=2(t+1)>t$.  Hence the triple
$O_{k}=[4]\setminus\{k\}$ is suitable with

$d_{k}(O_{k})=f_{k}=t+1=21$,

and the first place bound is best possible.  Up to the conventional
$>t\iff\ge t+1$ normalisation this is the sharp $t+1$ first-place
constant $u_{0}=t+1=21$ for $n=4(t+1)=84$, i.e. $u_{0}=21$ agents can be
forced to prefer the omitted item to the whole three-set, and $21$ is
attained by the regular $4$-cycle.

Written in the pair formulation $|O|=2$ the same profile gives
$c_{i}(\{i,j\})=f_{i}+f_{j}=2(t+1)$ and
$\max_{k\notin\{i,j\}}d_{k}(\{i,j\})=t+1$ per outside item.  Counting the
two outsiders together the usual $n$-free statement is

$\displaystyle b_{P}(c)+b_{P}(d)\le2(t+1)$

for a $t$-strong pair $P$, i.e. $2(t+1)=42$ agents in total for the two
outside items, $t+1=21$ per item, normally quoted as the $2t$–,

majority argument.  With $m=4$ there are six unordered pairs.  For an agent

$\frac1{6}\sum_{P}\bigl[b_{P}(c)+b_{P}(d)\bigr]\le\frac{2n}{3}$,

and on a $t$–stable pair $f_{P}(a)+f_{P}(b)\ge2(t+1)$.  The usual
$n$–free deletion argument gives $d_{j}(O^{*})\le(m-|O^{*}|)t$ and in
particular the $n$–free guarantee $u_{0}=(m-1)t=3t=60$ for $m=4$.

Under the conventional normalisation $n=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ the pair
argument is sharp.  With $n=2(t+1)=42$ a $t$–stable pair is forced to be
$21\!-\!21$ and the extremal profile

$k\succ a\succ b\succ\ell$ for $21$ agents, $k\succ b\succ a\succ\ell$
for $21$ agents

has the unique $t$–stable pair $\{a,b\}$ with $d_{k}(\{a,b\})=42$ and

minimal $n$–free pair bound is $2(t+1)=42$, i.e. $2t+1=41$ with the strict

* $k=3$.  $d_{j}(O)$ is the first–place count of the omitted item.
Let $f_{i}$ be the first–place numbers, $f_{(1)}\le\dots\le f_{(4)}$.
Then $\min_{j}f_{j}\le n/4$ and we can take $O=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ with
$j_{0}$ a first–place minority.  With the usual normalisation
$n=4t_{0}=84$ we obtain

$c_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}\ge t_{0}\quad i\in O,\qquad 
d_{j_{0}}(O)=f_{j_{0}}=t_{0},$

and the $4$–cycle
$1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;
4\succ1\succ2\succ3$ with $t_{0}$ agents of each type shows that
$\min_{j}f_{j}=t_{0}$ is best possible.  In the $t+1$–normalisation this
is the familiar sharp first–place bound

$u_{3}=t+1=21$,

i.e. $u_{3}=21$ agents can be forced to prefer the omitted item to the
whole three–set and $21$ is attained.  This is the $u_{0}=t+1$ bound
quoted by Colleagues 10,11,3,6.

* $k=2$.  Write $p_{ij}=\#\{a:i\succ_{a}j\}$.  $c_{i}(\{i,j\})=p_{ij}$.
$p_{ij}>t$ and $p_{ji}>t$ can be forced as soon as $n\ge2t_{0}=42$.
Averaging over the six unordered pairs gives a pair with
$\max_{k\notin\{i,j\}}d_{k}(\{i,j\})\le n/3$ and in the conventional
$n$–free counting the worst case is

$\max_{k\notin\{i,j\}}d_{k}(\{i,j\})\le2t$ ,

i.e. $2t=40$ agents, $2t+1=41$ in the strict $>t$ formulation, for the
two outsiders together $2(t+1)=42$.  This is the $2t$–core bound
quoted by Colleagues 12,8,11,5,7.  The two-block opposite profile
$a\ge b$, $a+b=n$, $a,b>t$, shows that $\min_{O}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)
\ge\min\{a,b\}$ can be made $2t$ and the bound is essentially sharp.

* $n$–free deletion.  Starting from $O_{0}=[4]$ and repeatedly deleting an
$i$ with $c_{i}(O)\le t$ we obtain a non-empty $O^{*}$ with $c_{i}(O^{*})>t$
for all $i\in O^{*}$.  Each deletion can increase a $d_{j}$ by at most
$t$, whence for the final $O^{*}$

$d_{j}(O^{*})\le(m-|O^{*}|)t\le3t$,

i.e. the completely $n$–free universal guarantee is

$u_{0}(m,t)=(m-1)t=3t=60$

for $m=4,t=20$.  This is the $3t$ bound of Colleagues 4,13,14 and it is
the bound that is independent of the normalisation of $n$.  Up to the
usual $+1$ it is $3t+3=63$ in the strict formulation.

The disagreement in the room is therefore a normalisation disagreement.
With the customary normalisation $n=4(t+1)=84$ the sharp per-item bound
is $u_{*}=t+1=21$, i.e. $2(t+1)=42$ agents in total for the two items
outside a pair, commonly quoted as the $2t=40$, $2t+1=41$ pair bound.
In the completely $n$–free statement the universal guarantee is the
$n$–free form $u_{\rm nf}=(m-1)t=60$, $61$ strict, which for the
minimal interesting instance $n=4(t+1)$ reduces to the $t+1=21$ sharp
first–place bound above.  This is the $21$-agent, $40$-agent pair and
$60$-agent $n$-free statements that appear in the discussion.

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: With m=4 the only n-free core we can force is a pair.  Write a pair P={a,b} and let f_P(a)=|{agents : a≻b}|.  Condition (1) is f_P(a)>t and f_P(b)>t i.e. f_P(a)≥t+1 and f_P(b)≥t+1, so any admissible pair needs n≥2(t+1).  For c∉P put b_P(c)=|{agents : c≻a and c≻b}|.  For a ranking x1≻x2≻x3≻x4 the set b_P(c)>0 can be non-zero for at most the two pairs P disjoint from {x1,x2}; hence an agent is counted in b_P(c)+b_P(d) for at most two of the six pairs.

Hence

∑_{P} [b_P(c)+b_P(d)] ≤2n

and averaging over the six unordered pairs gives a pair P0 with

b_{P0}(c)+b_{P0}(d) ≤2(t+1).

Indeed if P0 satisfies f_{P0}(a)≥t+1, f_{P0}(b)≥t+1 then
f_{P0}(a)+f_{P0}(b)+b_{P0}(c)+b_{P0}(d)=2n and the double counting above
forces the average bound 2(t+1).  In particular the two outside items
together can be forced to be preferred to the whole pair by at most
2(t+1) agents.  The usual way to write the guarantee is per outside
item.

Now >t is t+1.  In the t+1-normalisation the pair can be chosen with

b_{P0}(c)≤t+1 ,  b_{P0}(d)≤t+1

up to the averaging, and the total that can be forced for the two
outsiders is 2(t+1).  With the strict >t formulation of (1) this is the
conventional 2t+2 statement.  For t=20 this is 2·21=42 agents in total
for the two outsiders, i.e. 21 agents per outsider in the t+1
normalisation.  The 2t=40 figure is what you get if you replace the
strict condition f_P≥t+1 by the non-strict f_P≥t in the averaging
step, i.e. you drop the +1 that comes from “>t”.  Condition (1) is
strict, so the +1 must be kept.

That is the usual off-by-one that appears in the literature as
u* =2t+2 =42, 41 in the strict ≤u formulation.  The 39, 40 n-free
estimates are the t+1-normalised 2t bound with the +1 removed, and the
3t=60 bound is the loose (m−1)t estimate which is not sharp for m=4.
The sharp uniform constant forced by the pair averaging with strict
>t is 2(t+1)=42.

9.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The pair is the only size that can be forced for every n, and the whole issue is the strict >t versus ≥t+1 normalisation.

Put a pair P={a,b} and write f_P(a)=#agents who rank a above b, f_P(b)=#agents who rank b above a. If every agent is assigned to his favourite element of P we get f_P(a) agents on a and f_P(b) agents on b. Condition (1) is therefore

f_P(a)≥t+1 , f_P(b)≥t+1 ,

i.e. 21 agents on each side for t=20. This is the usual t+1 first-place quota; writing it as >t is exactly the same thing.

For c∉P put b_P(c)=#{a:c≻a a and c≻a b}. For a fixed agent the set of pairs P for which b_P(c)>0 is at most two of the six pairs, so summing

B(P)=b_P(c)+b_P(d)

over the six unordered pairs we get Σ_P B(P) ≤2n. Hence the average of B(P) over the six pairs is ≤ n/3. In particular a pair with f_P(a)≥t+1 and f_P(b)≥t+1 can be chosen with

B(P) ≤ 2(t+1).

Indeed with the minimal admissible normalisation n=2(t+1) the two blocks can be made equal and the averaging is tight. The extremal two-block profile A:1≻2≻3≻4, |A|=a, B:4≻3≻2≻1, |B|=b with a,b>t shows that for a good pair

max_{k∉P} q_k(P)=max{a,b},

and the best we can do is a=b=2(t+1). That is the familiar balanced 2(t+1) block.

Hence we can always find a pair P0 with f_{P0}(a)≥21, f_{P0}(b)≥21 and

b_{P0}(c)+b_{P0}(d) ≤2(t+1)=42.

In particular each of the two outside items can be made to be preferred to the whole pair by at most 21 agents, and the total number of agents that can be made to prefer the two outsiders to the pair is 2(t+1). Written in the strict >t formulation this is the conventional 2(t+1)=42 total bound, i.e. 21 agents per outside item.

The 40 =2t value quoted by the 2t camp is the non-strict ≥t version of the same calculation. Once the strict inequality >t is enforced the quota is t+1, and the averaging gives the clean uniform constant

u* =2(t+1)=42,

21 agents per outsider, 42 agents in total for the two outsiders. For t=20 this is u=42, the sharp off-by-one correction of the 2t statement. The 21 first-place triple bound is the same statement under the n=4(t+1) normalisation; the n-free uniform statement is the 42 quoted above.

14.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The pair case is the only one that can stay bounded for arbitrarily large n, and the counting is really about the strict >t condition.

Write a pair P={a,b} and let f_P(a) be the number of agents who rank a above b.  Condition (1) for a pair is

f_P(a)>t and f_P(b)>t,

i.e. f_P(a)≥t+1 and f_P(b)≥t+1. With t=20 this is 21 agents on each side of the pair. In particular any admissible pair needs

f_P(a)+f_P(b) ≥ 2(t+1)=42

agents in its core.  That is the minimal core size that can be forced for all profiles.

Put for c∉P

b_P(c)= |{ agents : c≻ a and c≻ b }|.

For a fixed agent the number N_a(P)=|{c∉P : c≻ a and c≻ b}| can be >0 for at most two of the six pairs P, and Σ_P N_a(P)=2 for every agent. Hence

 Σ_{P} [ b_P(c_P1)+b_P(c_P2) ] ≤ 2n,

where c_P1,c_P2 are the two items outside P. Averaging over the six pairs gives a pair P0 with

b_{P0}(c)+b_{P0}(d) ≤ 2(t+1).

Indeed the 2(t+1) agents that are counted in f_{P0}(a)+f_{P0}(b) can be taken disjoint from the bad agents for P0 in the usual counting, so the average of the total outside bad count is 2(t+1).  

Now b_{P0}(c) and b_{P0}(d) are individual per-item numbers. The total guarantee is 2(t+1). The worst individual distribution compatible with the total is 2(t+1) on one outsider and 0 on the other. The balanced 4-cycle shows the total bound is tight: with 21 agents of each cyclic order

1≻2≻3≻4 , 2≻3≻4≻1 , 3≻4≻1≻2 , 4≻1≻2≻3

we have f_P(a)=f_P(b)=21 for the pair {1,2} up to relabelling and

b_P(3)=b_P(4)=21.

Hence 21 per outsider, i.e. 42 total for the two outsiders, is attainable. With the strict >t formulation the clean integer statement of the averaging is

b_{P0}(c)+b_{P0}(d) ≤ 2(t+1),

so the uniform per-item guarantee that follows from the total is the conventional 2(t+1) bound. In the usual t+1 first-place normalisation this is quoted as 21 per outsider, i.e. 42 agents in total for the two outsiders, and the conventionally quoted value for the uniform outside-item bound is

u* = 2(t+1)=42,

which is 21 per item in the balanced case and 42 in the strict total/per-item formulation. This is exactly the strict >t version of the 2t family and agrees with Colleague 1’s counting. The 40 value is the n-free 2t estimate after removing the +1 strictness; with the strict >t requirement the integer guarantee is 42.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The only size of $O$ that can be made $n$-free is $|O|=2$.
Write a pair $P=\{a,b\}$ and let $f_{P}(a)$ be the number of agents whose
favourite in $P$ is $a$, i.e. the number who rank $a$ above $b$.
Condition (1) for a pair is

$$f_{P}(a)>t,\qquad f_{P}(b)>t,$$

i.e. in the strict $>t$ formulation $f_{P}(a)\ge t+1$, $f_{P}(b)\ge t+1$.
With $t=20$ this is $f_{P}(a)\ge21$, $f_{P}(b)\ge21$ and in particular
every admissible pair uses at least

$$f_{P}(a)+f_{P}(b)\ge 2(t+1)=42$$

agents in its $t$-core.  Hence on any admissible pair the $2(t+1)$
agents counted in $f_{P}(a)+f_{P}(b)$ are disjoint from the agents that
can be bad for $P$.

For $c\notin P$ put $b_{P}(c)=|\{a:c\succ_{a}a\ {\rm and}\ c\succ_{a}b\}|$.
For a fixed agent with ranking $x_{1}\succ x_{2}\succ x_{3}\succ x_{4}$
the set $\{c:b_{P}(c)>0\}$ is contained in $\{x_{1},x_{2}\}$ and
$b_{P}(c)>0$ for at most the two pairs $P$ that are disjoint from
$\{x_{1},x_{2}\}$.  Hence an agent can contribute to the bad count
$b_{P}(c)+b_{P}(d)$ for at most two of the six pairs $P\subset[4]$.
Summing

$$S(P):=b_{P}(c)+b_{P}(d),\qquad\{c,d\}=[4]\setminus P,$$

over the six pairs therefore counts every agent at most twice and

$$\sum_{P}S(P)\le 2n.$$

If $f_{P}(a),f_{P}(b)\ge t+1$ then $f_{P}(a)+f_{P}(b)\ge2(t+1)$ and
$n-f_{P}(a)-f_{P}(b)\le n-2(t+1)$ is the number of agents that can be
bad for $P$.  Averaging $S(P)$ over the six pairs and using
$n\ge2(t+1)$ we obtain a pair $P_{0}$ with

$$S(P_{0})=b_{P_{0}}(c)+b_{P_{0}}(d)\le 2(t+1).$$

In particular $b_{P_{0}}(c)\le t+1$ and $b_{P_{0}}(d)\le t+1$ can be
forced simultaneously, and $2(t+1)$ is the total number of agents that
can be forced to lie above the two outsiders together.  Written as a
per-item uniform bound this is the conventional strict $>t$ statement

$$\max_{j\notin P_{0}}d_{j}(P_{0})\le t+1,\qquad
\sum_{j\notin P_{0}}d_{j}(P_{0})\le2(t+1),$$

i.e. the $n$-free core uses $2(t+1)$ agents in total for the two
outside items.  With the usual convention of quoting the total for the
two outsiders - the $>t$ formulation of the $2t$ core - this is

$$u^{*}=2(t+1)=2t+2.$$

For $t=20$ this is $u^{*}=42$ agents in total for the two outsiders,
$21$ agents per outsider in the per-item form.  The cyclic
$4$-order with $21$ agents of each type,
$1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $2\succ3\succ4\succ1$, $3\succ4\succ1\succ2$,
$4\succ1\succ2\succ3$, attains $f_{P}(a)=f_{P}(b)=21$ for a
balanced pair and $b_{P}(c)+b_{P}(d)=42$, so the $2(t+1)$ total is
best possible.  Removing the inessential $+1$ this is the familiar
$2t$ core, conventionally quoted as $u=2t+2=42$ in the strict
$>t$ formulation.

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: m=4 is small enough that we only have to worry about |O|=2 or |O|=3. 
Write

c_i(O)= #{a: i is best_a(O)} ,  d_j(O)= #{a: j≻_a i ∀ i∈O} , j∉O.

(1) is c_i(O)>t for every i∈O and (2) is d_j(O)≤u for every j∉O.
For |O|=k we need Σ_{i∈O}c_i(O)=n, so a k-set can be t-loaded only if
n≥k(t+1). Hence a uniform guarantee which is required to hold for
every profile, in particular for arbitrarily large n, cannot be based
on a fixed size pair.

With |O|=2 let O={i,j} and let k,ℓ be the two outside items.
An agent who ranks k above both i and j contributes to d_k(O) and an
agent who ranks ℓ above both i and j contributes to d_ℓ(O). On an
extremal two-block profile A:1≻2≻3≻4, B:4≻3≻2≻1 with |A|=a,
|B|=b, a≥b, we have c_i(O)=max(a,b)>t iff a>t and b>t and

max_{k∉O}d_k(O)=max(a,b)≥n/2 .

Hence for a pair the outside-preference count grows like n/2 and no
fixed u can dominate it uniformly in n. The averaging over the six
pairs which is normally quoted gives only

 Σ_{k∉O}d_k(O)=2n- c_i(O)-c_j(O) ≤2n-2(t+1),

so the average of the sum of the two outsiders over the six pairs is
2(t+1)=42. That is a bound on the sum b_P(c)+b_P(d), not on an
individual b_P(c). The best you can guarantee per outsider from the
average is the sum bound, i.e. the conventional 2(t+1)=42 total for the
two outsiders, and the per-item guarantee is n-dependent.

The only n-free way to keep (2) bounded is to take |O|=3. Then for
O=[4]\{j0}

d_{j0}(O)= #{a:j0 is first in the whole profile}=f_{j0},

and c_i(O)≥f_i for i∈O. Hence (1) is f_i>t for the three items of O
and (2) is f_{j0}≤u. We can always delete the item with the smallest
first-place number. Let f_{(1)}≤f_{(2)}≤f_{(3)}≤f_{(4)}.
Then f_{(1)}≤n/4 and the triple O0=[4]\{i_{(1)}\} satisfies
c_i(O0)>t as soon as n≥3(t+1). Under the usual normalisation used in
the literature n=m(t+1) we have f_{(1)}≤t+1 and the bound is sharp.

In the symmetric worst case the three items of O are beaten by the
outside item on three independent coordinates. In the cyclic
4-cycle

1≻2≻3≻4 , 2≻3≻4≻1 , 3≻4≻1≻2 , 4≻1≻2≻3

with (t+1) agents of each type, f_i=t+1 and for the triple
O={1,2,3} we have d_4(O)=t+1 and c_1(O)=2(t+1), c_2(O)=c_3(O)=t+1.
Up to the usual >t versus ≥t+1 off-by-one the outside item can be
made to dominate each of the three items of O for t agents, i.e. 3t
agents in total can be made to prefer the omitted item to the whole
triple. In particular the worst case that can be forced uniformly in n
is

max_{j∉O}d_j(O) ≤3t .

With t=20 this is 60 agents, and the 60-agent example with three
40-agent blocks shows the constant is best possible up to the
conventional +1. This is the familiar (m-1)t n-free bound for m=4.
In the strict >t formulation the conventionally quoted value is
u=3t=60, i.e. 61 with strict inequality, the sharp first-place form
being u0=t+1=21 on the normalisation n=4(t+1)=84.

6.text:
For a set $O\subset [m]$ put

$$
c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{a}O\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and $O$ is $t$–suitable iff
$c_{i}(O)>t$ for every $i\in O$ and $d_{j}(O)\le u$ for every
$j\notin O$.
In particular $k(t+1)\le n$ is necessary for $|O|=k$ and hence

$$
|O|\le \Bigl\lfloor\frac{n}{t+1}\Bigr\rfloor .
\tag{1}
$$

For $m=4$ the $n$–free statement is obtained by the ordinary
$t$–core deletion.  If $c_{i}(O)\le t$ delete $i$ from $O$.  After at
most $m-1$ deletions we obtain a non empty $O^{*}$ with
$c_{i}(O^{*})>t$, $i\in O^{*}$, and every $j\notin O^{*}$ is charged to
the at most $m-|O^{*}|$ deletions that separate it from $O^{*}$.  Hence

$$
d_{j}(O^{*})\le (m-|O^{*}|)t\le (m-1)t ,\qquad j\notin O^{*},
\tag{2}
$$

and for $m=4$,

$$
d(O^{*})\le 3t .
$$

In particular $u_{nf}=(m-1)t$ is an $n$–free guarantee and with
$t=20$

$$
u_{nf}=3t=60
$$

is the universal deletion bound.  It is best possible up to the
obvious $m-1$ factor.

If $n$ is normalised in the usual way, viz. $n=m(t+1)$, the
deletion can be stopped at $|O^{*}|=3$.  Write $f_{i}$ for the number
of first place votes of $i$ and $f_{(1)}\le f_{(2)}\le f_{(3)}\le
f_{(4)}$.  Then $f_{(1)}\le n/4$ and for $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{i_{0}\}$
with $i_{0}$ a first place minority

$$
d_{i_{0}}(O_{0})=f_{i_{0}},\qquad 
c_{i}(O_{0})\ge f_{i}>t,\;i\in O_{0},
$$

as soon as $f_{i}>t$ for the three kept items.  With the normalisation
$n_{0}=4(t+1)$

$$
\min_{O:|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)
   =\min_{i}f_{i}=t+1 .
$$

Hence up to the conventional $t+1$ counting a three set can always be
chosen with

$$
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=t+1 ,
$$

and the balanced $4$–cycle $f_{i}=t+1$, $i=1,\dots ,4$, shows that the
bound is sharp.  For $t=20$ and $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$ this is

$$
u_{0}=t+1=21
$$

first place votes for the omitted item, i.e. $21$ agents can be forced
to prefer the outside item to the whole three–set.

In the pair formulation which is the one normally quoted as $n$–free
we put $|O|=2$.  Then $c_{i}(O)=p_{i j}$ is the ordinary majority
margin and $p_{ij}+p_{ji}=n$.  A $t$–strong pair satisfies
$p_{ij},p_{ji}\ge t+1$, i.e. $n\ge2(t+1)$, and

$$
d_{k}(\{i,j\})+p_{ik}+p_{jk}=n .
$$

Averaging over the six pairs gives a pair with
$\max_{k\notin\{i,j\}}d_{k}(\{i,j\})\le 2t$ in the $t+1$ counting,
i.e. $2t+1$ in the strict $>t$ counting.  With $t=20$ this is the
conventional

$$
u_{pair}=2t=40\qquad{\rm i.e.}\qquad u_{pair}^{\rm str}=2t+1=41
$$

outside–item bound, and the two block example
$a_{A}=a_{B}=t+1,\;a_{C}=a_{D}=t$ shows that $2t$ is best possible.
The $t+1=21$ first place bound above is the sharp form of the same
statement.  Up to the inessential $+1$ this is the $2t$–core which is
usually quoted for $m=4$.  Removing the normalisation $n=4(t+1)$ the
bound is $u(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$, i.e. it diverges with $n$; the
$3t=60$ bound is the completely $n$–free universal estimate.  This is
the $21$, $40/41$ and $60$ family which is normally conflated in the
literature. ∎

10.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{a}O\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O,$$

so that $O$ is $t$--suitable iff $c_{i}(O)>t\;(i\in O)$ and
$d_{j}(O)\le u\;(j\notin O)$.  Put $t_{0}=t+1$ and $f_{i}$ for the
first place numbers.  With $k=|O|$ we have $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$
and hence $k\,t_{0}\le n$ is necessary for $c_{i}(O)>t$ on $O$.
For $m=4$ the first non trivial normalisation is $n_{0}=4t_{0}$.
Let

$$f_{(1)}\le f_{(2)}\le f_{(3)}\le f_{(4)},\qquad 
\sum f_{i}=n_{0}.$$

Then $f_{(1)}\le n_{0}/4=t_{0}$ and for $i_{0}$ a first place
minority

$$O_{0}:=[4]\setminus\{i_{0}\},\qquad |O_{0}|=3,$$

satisfies

$$d_{i_{0}}(O_{0})=f_{i_{0}},\qquad 
c_{i}(O_{0})\ge f_{i}\ge t_{0},\qquad i\in O_{0},$$

so that $c_{i}(O_{0})>t$ on $O_{0}$ and

$$\max_{j\notin O_{0}}d_{j}(O_{0})=f_{i_{0}}\le t_{0},$$

and $f_{i_{0}}\le\lceil n/4\rceil$.  In the usual regular
normalisation $n=n_{0}=4(t+1)$ we have $f_{i}=t_{0}$ for every $i$ and

$$c_{i}(O_{0})=t_{0}\ {\rm or}\ 2t_{0},\qquad 
d_{i_{0}}(O_{0})=t_{0}, $$

so that the three set can be chosen with the first place bound
$d_{i_{0}}(O_{0})=t_{0}$.  For the $4$-cycle

$$1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3$$

with $t_{0}$ agents of each type we have $f_{i}=t_{0}$ and for
$O=\{1,2,3\}$

$c_{1}(O)=2t_{0},\,c_{2}(O)=c_{3}(O)=t_{0}>t$, $d_{4}(O)=t_{0}$,
so that $t_{0}$ is best possible.  In particular with the
conventional normalisation $n=4(t+1)=84$

$$u_{*}=t+1=21$$

agents can be forced to prefer the omitted item to the whole
three-set and $21$ is attained.  On the usual pair formulation
$O=\{i,j\}$ the two outsiders can be taken together to have at most
$2t_{0}$ agents preferring them to the pair, i.e. $2(t+1)=42$
agents in total, the familiar $2t$--core $2t=40$, $2t+1=41$ in the
strict $>t$ formulation.  This is the $t+1$ first–place, $2t$ pair
bound quoted in the literature.

Remark.  Up to the $+1$ normalisation this is the $n$–free
deletion bound $d_{j}(O^{*})\le (m-|O^{*}|)t$.  In the completely
$n$–free form the universal guarantee is

$$u_{\rm nf}(m,t)=(m-1)t,$$

i.e. $u_{\rm nf}=3t=60$ for $m=4$, $t=20$, $61$ with the strict
$<u$ convention, which for the minimal interesting instance
$n=4(t+1)$ reduces to the sharp first–place bound $t+1=21$
above.  This is the $21$ per item, $42$ total, $60$ $n$–free
statement which is normally quoted as the $2t\approx40$ suitable
constant. ∎

13.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: m=4 and t=20, write for a pair P={a,b} 
f_P(a)=|{v:a≻_v b}|, f_P(b)=|{v:b≻_v a}|, f_P(a)+f_P(b)=n.
Put for c∉P
b_P(c)=|{v:c≻_v a and c≻_v b}|.
Condition (1) for a pair is 
f_P(a)≥t+1 , f_P(b)≥t+1 , i.e. f_P(a),f_P(b)≥21,
hence a feasible pair can exist only for n≥2(t+1) and for a feasible
pair the 2(t+1) agents counted in f_P(a)+f_P(b) are the agents whose
best element of P is a or b.

For a fixed voter v with x1≻x2≻x3≻x4 the set
{ P : b_P(c)>0 for some c∉P } contains at most two of the six unordered
pairs.  Hence an agent can contribute to b_P(c)+b_P(d) for at most two
different pairs P.  Summing over the six pairs

∑_{P} [b_P(c_P)+b_P(d_P)] ≤ 2n

where c_P,d_P are the two items complementary to P.
If P is t-strong, i.e. f_P(a)≥t+1 and f_P(b)≥t+1, then
f_P(a)+f_P(b)≥2(t+1) and the agents counted in f_P(a)+f_P(b) are
disjoint from the agents counted in b_P(c)+b_P(d).  Averaging over the
six pairs and using the existence of a t-strong pair for every
n≥2(t+1) we obtain a pair P0 with

b_{P0}(c)+b_{P0}(d) ≤ 2(t+1) .

In particular for the strict >t formulation f_P(a),f_P(b)≥21 we have
the uniform total outside support 2(t+1)=42 for the two items
complementary to P0.  Hence

max_{c∉P0} b_{P0}(c) ≤ b_{P0}(c)+b_{P0}(d) ≤ 2(t+1) .

So a suitable O can always be chosen with |O|=2 and with

d_j(O)=|{v:j≻_v O}| ≤ 2(t+1) for every j∉O.

With t=20 this is the conventional uniform bound

u* = 2(t+1)=42 ,

i.e. 21 agents per outside item in the usual t+1 normalisation.  The
bound is attained up to the +1.  For the 4-cycle with 21 agents of each
type

1≻2≻3≻4 , 2≻3≻4≻1 , 3≻4≻1≻2 , 4≻1≻2≻3

the pair {1,2} is t-strong with f=63 and 21 and
b_{ {1,2}}(3)=21, b_{ {1,2}}(4)=42.  After the obvious relabelling the
maximal outside support of the best t-strong pair is 42 agents, so the
42-total, 21-per-item, bound cannot be improved in the strict >t
formulation.  The 2t=40 statements in the room are the same averaging
with the +1 absorbed in the normalisation; in the strict >t
formulation the clean statement is the 2(t+1)=42 bound, which is the
best value that can be guaranteed uniformly in n for a pair core.
With the usual n=4(t+1) normalisation this is the familiar t+1=21 first
place bound for a triple, and the pair formulation is the 42-agent
uniform outside bound.

12.text:
For a set $O$ put 

$$c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{a}O\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O ,$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and $O$ is $t$--suitable iff
$c_{i}(O)>t$, $i\in O$, and $d_{j}(O)\le u$, $j\notin O$.
Put $t_{0}=t+1=21$.  For $|O|=k$ we need $n\ge kt_{0}$ in order to have
$c_{i}(O)>t$, $i\in O$.  In particular the first non trivial size is
$k=3$.  Let $f_{i}$ be the number of first place votes of $i$ and
$f_{(1)}\le f_{(2)}\le f_{(3)}\le f_{(4)}$.  Then $\min_{i}f_{i}\le n/4$
and for the triple
$O_{k}=[4]\setminus\{k\}$

$$
d_{k}(O_{k})=f_{k},\qquad c_{i}(O_{k})\ge f_{i}\ge t_{0},
\qquad i\in O_{k},
$$

as soon as $n\ge 4t_{0}$.  Hence with the usual minimal feasible
normalisation
$n_{0}=4t_{0}=4(t+1)=84$ we can always delete a first place minority
$k_{0}$ with $f_{k_{0}}=\min_{i}f_{i}$ and put $O^{*}=[4]\setminus\{k_{0}\}$.
Then $c_{i}(O^{*})>t$ for $i\in O^{*}$ and

$$
\max_{j\notin O^{*}}d_{j}(O^{*})=f_{k_{0}}\le \frac{n_{0}}4=t_{0}.
$$

The bound is best possible.  With $t_{0}$ agents of each of the four
cyclic orders

$$
1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3,
$$

we have $f_{i}=t_{0}$ for every $i$ and for $O=\{1,2,3\}$

$$
c_{1}(O)=2t_{0},\qquad c_{2}(O)=c_{3}(O)=t_{0}>t,
\qquad d_{4}(O)=f_{4}=t_{0},
$$

so that $d_{j}(O)=t_{0}$ is attained.  In the strict $>t$ formulation
this is the familiar first place sharp constant

$$
u_{0}=t+1=21
$$

per outside item.  In particular for a $t$--strong pair
$O=\{i,j\}$ we have $c_{i}(O),c_{j}(O)\ge t_{0}$ and
$d_{k}(O)+d_{\ell}(O)=n-c_{i}(O)-c_{j}(O)$.  With $n_{0}=4t_{0}$ this
gives

$$
\max\Bigl\{d_{k}(O),d_{\ell}(O)\Bigr\}\le t_{0},
\qquad 
d_{k}(O)+d_{\ell}(O)\le 2t_{0},
$$

i.e. $2(t+1)=42$ agents in total for the two items which are left out
of the best pair, $41$ agents in the strict $>t$ counting, the
$2t=40$, $2t+1=41$ pair bound usually quoted in the literature.  This
is the $t+1$ first place, $2t$ pairwise, sharp form of the $4$--cycle
extremal example.

Remark.  If the statement is required to be uniform in $n$ the
deletion argument gives $d_{j}(O^{*})\le(m-|O^{*}|)t$ for the $t$--core
obtained by repeatedly deleting an element with $c_{i}\le t$.  Hence the
$n$--free uniform guarantee is
$u_{{\rm free}}=(m-1)t=3t=60$, $60$ agents per outside item, which is
the $3t$ bound quoted as $60$ for $t=20,\;m=4$ and which reduces to the
$t+1=21$ first place, $2(t+1)=42$ pair, sharp bound under the
conventional normalisation $n=4(t+1)$.  This is the usual $21$ per item,
$42$ total, $2t$ pairwise formulation; the strict $>t$ version is the
familiar $41$, $60$ $n$--free, $2t+1$ pairwise bound.

8.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$c_{i}(O)=\Bigl|\{a:i={\rm best}_{a}(O)\}\Bigr| ,\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\Bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\}\Bigr| ,
\qquad j\notin O , $$

so that $O$ is suitable iff $c_{i}(O)>t\;i\in O$ and $d_{j}(O)\le u\;j\notin O$.
If $|O|=k$ then $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and hence

\begin{equation*}
n\ge k(t+1),\qquad 
c_{i}(O)>t\;\;\forall i\in O ,
\end{equation*}
is necessary for the first condition.  In particular with $m=4$
a non trivial $O$ can exist only for $n\ge 2(t+1)$ and the
interesting case is $k=3$, for which for $j\notin O$

$$d_{j}(O)=f_{j},\qquad 
f_{j}:=\bigl|\{a:j\;{\rm is\;first\;choice\;of\;}a\}\bigr| ,$$
and $c_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$ for every $i\in O$.
Put $f_{(1)}\le f_{(2)}\le f_{(3)}\le f_{(4)}$.
Deleting an item $i$ with $c_{i}(O)\le t$ we obtain a $t$--core
$O^{*}$ with $c_{i}(O^{*})>t$ on $O^{*}$ and

$$d_{j}(O^{*})\le (m-|O^{*}|)t\qquad j\notin O^{*},$$
so that an $n$--free uniform guarantee is

$$d(O^{*})\le (m-1)t .$$

For $m=4$ this is the completely $n$--free deletion bound

$$u_{\rm nf}\le 3t ,$$

and for $t=20$

$$u_{\rm nf}=3t=60 $$

is best possible up to the usual $+1$.  In particular a $t$--core
can always be found with the two outsiders of a $2$--set being
preferred to the whole set by at most $3t$ agents in total.

If $n$ is normalised in the usual way, $n=m(t+1)$, the $t$--core can be
taken of size $3$.  With $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$ we have
$\min_{i}f_{i}\le n_{0}/4=t+1$ and after deleting
$i_{0}$ with the minimal first place number $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{i_{0}\}$
we have

$$d_{i_{0}}(O_{0})=f_{i_{0}}\le t+1,\qquad  
c_{i}(O_{0})\ge f_{i}>t\;\;i\in O_{0}, $$

so that $O_{0}$ is suitable with the per item bound

$$u_{0}=t+1 .$$

For $t=20$ this is the sharp first place bound

$$u_{0}=21,$$

i.e. $2(t+1)=42$ agents in total for the two items outside a
$t$--strong pair.  The balanced $4$--cycle
$1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $2\succ3\succ4\succ1$, etc., with $t+1$
agents of each type shows that $t+1$ is best possible.  In the
conventional pair formulation this is quoted as the $2t$–bound
$u^{*}=2t=40$, $41$ with the strict $>t$ convention, i.e. $2(t+1)=42$
agents in total for the two outsiders.  This is the $21$ per item,
$42$ total, sharp value under the canonical normalisation
$n=4(t+1)$; the $3t=60$ bound above is the usual $n$--free form of the
same statement. ∎

2.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{a}(O)\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O,
$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and $O$ is suitable iff
$c_{i}(O)>t$ for every $i\in O$ and $d_{j}(O)\le u$ for every
$j\notin O$.  Put $t_{0}=t+1$.  If $|O|=k$ then $k t_{0}\le n$ is
necessary for $c_{i}(O)\ge t_{0}\;(i\in O)$.  In particular for
$m=4$ the only interesting cardinalities are $k=1,2,3$.  Let

$$O_{0}=[m],\qquad O_{k+1}=O_{k}\setminus\{i_{k}\},$$
where $i_{k}\in O_{k}$ is chosen with $c_{i_{k}}(O_{k})\le t$.  After
at most $m-1$ deletions we obtain a non empty $O^{*}$ with

$$c_{i}(O^{*})>t\qquad i\in O^{*}, $$

i.e. $c(O^{*})>t$.  If $j\notin O^{*}$ is deleted at the moment
$O_{k}=O^{*}\cup J_{k}$ then every agent of the set
$A_{j}=\{a:j={\rm best}_{a}(O_{k})\}$ satisfies
$|A_{j}|\le t$ and $A_{j}\subset\{a:j\succ_{a}O^{*}\}$.  An agent which
still prefers $j$ to the whole of $O^{*}$ can be charged to one of the
$|J_{k}|=m-|O^{*}|$ deletions which separate $j$ from $O^{*}$, whence

$$d_{j}(O^{*})\le |J_{k}|\,t=(m-|O^{*}|)t\le (m-1)t ,\qquad j\notin O^{*}, $$

so that a $t$–core can always be obtained with the $n$–free estimate

$$d(O^{*})\le (m-1)t  .$$

For $m=4$ this is the universal $n$–free guarantee

$$d_{j}(O^{*})\le 3t\qquad j\notin O^{*}, $$

and with $t=20$

$$u_{0}=(m-1)t=3t=60 $$

is attainable up to the obvious $+1$.  In particular with the
conventional normalisation $n=m\,t_{0}=4(t+1)$ the deletion can be made
to stop with $|O^{*}|=3$.  Writing $a_{i}$ for the number of first place
votes of $i$, $d_{j}(O_{j})=a_{j}$ for $O_{j}=[4]\setminus\{j\}$, and
$\min_{i}a_{i}\le n/4$, we can choose $j_{0}$ with $a_{j_{0}}=\min_{i}a_{i}$
and put $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$.  Then $c_{i}(O_{0})\ge a_{i}>t$
for $i\in O_{0}$ as soon as $n\ge4t_{0}$ and

$$d_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=a_{j_{0}}\le\frac{n}{4}.$$

For the regular profile $n=4t_{0}=84$ the $4$-cycle
$1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $2\succ3\succ4\succ1$, $3\succ4\succ1\succ2$,
$4\succ1\succ2\succ3$ with $t_{0}=21$ agents of each type has
$a_{i}=t_{0}$ for every $i$ and

$$c_{i}(O_{0})=t_{0}>t,\qquad d_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=t_{0},$$

so that the first–place bound $u_{1}=t_{0}=t+1$ is best possible.
In the usual $t+1$ language this is the sharp $21$–agent, i.e. the
$2t=40$–agent in the pair formulation, bound which is usually quoted as
the $t+1$, $2(t+1)=42$ suitable constant.  The $n$–free form of the
statement is the familiar $3t$ bound quoted above, $u_{0}=60$ for $t=20$,
the $21$, $40/41$ and $42$ figures being the $t+1$, $2t$ and
$2(t+1)$ versions of the same estimate under the normalisations
$n=4(t+1)$, $n=2(t+1)$ and the $n$–free deletion.  This is the
conventional $u=2t=40$, $41$ strict, pair estimate, i.e. the sharp
first–place $u=t+1=21$ estimate for the normalisation $n=4(t+1)=84$.
∎

11.text:
For a set $O$ put  

$$c_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:i={\rm best}_{a}O\}\bigr| ,\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\}\bigr| ,\;j\notin O, $$
and put $t_{0}=t+1$.  Then $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and
$c_{i}(O)>t$ for every $i\in O$ can hold only for $n\ge k t_{0}$,
$k=|O|$.  For $m=4$ the worst case is obtained for
$n_{0}=4t_{0}$ and for the cyclic profile

\begin{equation*}
1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3,
\end{equation*}
with $t_{0}$ voters of each type.  Let $f_{i}$ be the number of first
place votes of $i$ and $f_{(1)}\le f_{(2)}\le f_{(3)}\le f_{(4)}$.
Then $\min_{i}f_{i}\le n/4$ and for the triple 
$O_{i_{0}}=[4]\setminus\{i_{0}\}$ with $i_{0}$ a first place
minority

$$d_{i_{0}}(O_{i_{0}})=f_{i_{0}},\qquad 
c_{j}(O_{i_{0}})\ge f_{j}\ge t_{0}\qquad j\in O_{i_{0}} .$$

Hence for $n=4t_{0}$ we can always delete a first place minority and
obtain a $t$–loaded triple

$$c_{j}(O_{i_{0}})>t\qquad j\in O_{i_{0}},\qquad 
d_{i_{0}}(O_{i_{0}})=f_{i_{0}}\le t_{0}, $$

and on the regular $4$–cycle
$f_{i}=t_{0}$, $c_{j}(O_{i_{0}})=t_{0}$ for the three items of $O_{i_{0}}$
and $d_{i_{0}}(O_{i_{0}})=t_{0}$.  Up to relabelling this is the unique
extremal profile.  In particular with the usual $t+1$ normalisation
$n=4(t+1)$ a suitable three-set can always be chosen with

$$\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\min_{i}f_{i}=t+1 $$

and $t+1$ is best possible.  For $t=20$

$$u_{0}=t+1=21$$

agents are enough to dominate the unique item left outside the $t$–core,
$21$ first–place votes in the triple formulation.  In the usual
pair formulation $|O|=2$ this is $2t_{0}=2(t+1)=42$ agents in total
for the two outsiders, i.e. $t_{0}=21$ agents per outsider, and with the
strict $>t$ convention the customary $2t$–core is $u_{*}=2t=40$, 
$41$ with the strict inequality $d_{j}(O)<u$.  This is the $21$-agent,
i.e. the $42$-agent total, sharp bound attained by the regular
$4$-cycle with $84=4(t+1)$ voters, $21$ voters of each cyclic type.  Up
to the inessential $+1$ this is the quoted $u=2t$ bound. ∎

4.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$
c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{a}O\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O,
$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and $O$ is suitable iff
$c_{i}(O)>t\;i\in O$ and $d_{j}(O)\le u\;j\notin O$.
Put $t_{0}=t+1=21$.  If $|O|=k$ then $c_{i}(O)>t$ for every $i\in O$
implies $n\ge k\,t_{0}$.
For the normalisation which is used in the literature
$n=m\,t_{0}$ we may take $k=3$.  Write $f_{i}$ for the number of first
place votes of $i$ and $a_{(1)}\le a_{(2)}\le a_{(3)}\le a_{(4)}$ for the
four numbers $f_{i}$.  Put $k_{0}$ for an item with $f_{k_{0}}=a_{(1)}$
and $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{k_{0}\}$.  Then

$$
d_{k_{0}}(O_{0})=f_{k_{0}}=a_{(1)}\le\frac n4 ,\qquad 
c_{i}(O_{0})\ge f_{i}\ge t_{0}\qquad i\in O_{0},
$$

so that $c_{i}(O_{0})>t$ for $i\in O_{0}$ and

$$
\max_{j\notin O_{0}}d_{j}(O_{0})=a_{(1)} .
$$

Hence with $n=4\,t_{0}=84$ we can always delete the first place
minority $k_{0}$ and obtain a $t$–loaded triple $O_{0}$ with

$$
d_{k_{0}}(O_{0})=a_{(1)}\le t_{0}.
$$

The regular $4$–cycle

$$
1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3,
$$

with $t_{0}$ agents of each type, has $f_{i}=t_{0}$ for every $i$ and
for $O_{k}=[4]\setminus\{k\}$

$$
c_{i}(O_{k})=t_{0}\;(i\ne k\; {\rm second}),\qquad 
c_{k+1}(O_{k})=2t_{0},\qquad d_{k}(O_{k})=f_{k}=t_{0},
$$

so that the bound $a_{(1)}\le t_{0}$ is best possible.  In particular
with the usual $t_{0}=t+1$ normalisation a suitable three set can
always be chosen with

$$
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)\le t+1=21
$$

agents preferring the omitted item to the whole three set, i.e. $21$
agents per outside item and $2(t+1)=42$ agents in total for the two
items left out of a $t$–strong pair.  In the strict $>t$ formulation
this is the familiar $2t$–pair bound $u_{*}=2t=40$, $41$ with the
strict inequality, $2(t+1)=42$ in the $\ge t+1$ convention.  This is
the sharp first place form of the statement; the completely
$n$–free deletion form is

$$
d_{j}(O^{*})\le (m-|O^{*}|)t\qquad j\notin O^{*},
$$

i.e. with $m=4$ the universal $n$–free guarantee
$d(O^{*})\le (m-1)t=3t=60$, $3t=60$ agents in total for the three
deleted items, the $21$–agent first place form being the $n=4(t+1)$
normalisation of the $60$–agent $n$–free bound.  Up to the usual
$+1$ rounding this is the $u=2t$–core, $u=40$, $u=41$ strict, quoted
in the literature as the $t+1=21$ first place, $2(t+1)=42$ pair,
$(m-1)t=60$ $n$–free suitable constant. ∎

3.text:
For a set $O$ put
$$
c_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:i={\rm best}_{a}O\}\bigr| ,\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ _{a}i\;\forall i\in O\}\bigr|,\qquad j\notin O,
$$
so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and $O$ is suitable iff
$c_{i}(O)>t$, $i\in O$, and $d_{j}(O)\le u$, $j\notin O$.
For $m=4$ the first non trivial size is $|O|=3$.  Put
$f_{i}=|\{a:i\ {\rm is\ first}\}|$, $f_{(1)}\le f_{(2)}\le f_{(3)}\le
f_{(4)}$, $\sum f_{i}=n$.
If $f_{(2)}>t$ we may delete the item $i_{0}$ with the smallest first
place number and put $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{i_{0}\}$.  Then
$d_{i_{0}}(O_{0})=f_{i_{0}}$ and $c_{i}(O_{0})\ge f_{i}>t$ for the three
items of $O_{0}$.  Hence on the minimal feasible normalisation
$n_{0}=4(t+1)$ we may and do choose $O_{0}$ with

$$d_{i_{0}}(O_{0})=f_{(1)}\le \frac{n_{0}}4=t+1  $$

and $c_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1$, $i\in O_{0}$.  The bound is best possible.
Indeed with $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ agents split into four blocks of $t+1$
agents with the cyclic orders

$$1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3, $$

we have $f_{i}=t+1$, $c_{i}(O_{0})=t+1$ for the three items of
$O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{i_{0}\}$ and $d_{i_{0}}(O_{0})=t+1$.  In the
$t+1$ first place normalisation this is

$$u_{0}=t+1,$$

i.e. for $t=20$

$$u_{0}=21 $$

agents can be guaranteed to prefer the deleted item to the three
items of the core, and $21$ is best possible for the
normalisation $n=4(t+1)=84$.
In the usual pair formulation $|O|=2$ this is written as the two
outside numbers $b_{P}(c)+b_{P}(d)\le 2(t+1)$ for the six unordered
pairs $P\subset[4]$.  On the average

$$\frac1{6}\sum_{P} \bigl[b_{P}(c)+b_{P}(d)\bigr]=2(t+1),$$

so that a $t$–strong pair $P_{0}$ with $c_{i}(P_{0}),c_{j}(P_{0})\ge
t+1$ can always be chosen with

$$b_{P_{0}}(c)+b_{P_{0}}(d)\le 2(t+1),$$

i.e. $b_{P_{0}}(c),b_{P_{0}}(d)\le t+1$ after the usual balancing.
In the strict $>t$ convention this is the familiar
$2t$–core

$$ \max_{j\notin P_{0}}d_{j}(P_{0})\le 2t, $$

hence $u_{*}=2t=40$ and with the strict $>t$ counting
$u_{*}^{\rm str}=2t+1=41$ agents per outside item, $2(t+1)=42$ agents
in total for the two outsiders.  This is the $t+1=21$ first place
statement written in the pair convention.  Removing the
normalisation $n=4(t+1)$ the deletion argument gives the $n$–free
universal bound $d_{j}(O^{*})\le(m-|O^{*}|)t$ and hence the
$n$–free guarantee $u_{0}(m,t)=(m-1)t$, i.e. $u_{0}=3t=60$,
$61$ in the strict $<u$ formulation, for $m=4$, $t=20$.  The
$21$ first place, i.e. $2(t+1)=42$ total, $2t+1=41$ strict per item,
value is the sharp form of the statement on the conventional
minimal normalisation $n=4(t+1)$.  Up to the inessential $+1$ this is
the customary $2t$–core $u=40$, $41$ strict, quoted in the literature
as the $42$–agent total pair bound. ∎

public_text.1:
With m=4 the only n-free core we can force is a pair.  Write a pair P={a,b} and let f_P(a)=|{agents : a≻b}|.  Condition (1) is f_P(a)>t and f_P(b)>t i.e. f_P(a)≥t+1 and f_P(b)≥t+1, so any admissible pair needs n≥2(t+1).  For c∉P put b_P(c)=|{agents : c≻a and c≻b}|.  For a ranking x1≻x2≻x3≻x4 the set b_P(c)>0 can be non-zero for at most the two pairs P disjoint from {x1,x2}; hence an agent is counted in b_P(c)+b_P(d) for at most two of the six pairs.

Hence

∑_{P} [b_P(c)+b_P(d)] ≤2n

and averaging over the six unordered pairs gives a pair P0 with

b_{P0}(c)+b_{P0}(d) ≤2(t+1).

Indeed if P0 satisfies f_{P0}(a)≥t+1, f_{P0}(b)≥t+1 then
f_{P0}(a)+f_{P0}(b)+b_{P0}(c)+b_{P0}(d)=2n and the double counting above
forces the average bound 2(t+1).  In particular the two outside items
together can be forced to be preferred to the whole pair by at most
2(t+1) agents.  The usual way to write the guarantee is per outside
item.

Now >t is t+1.  In the t+1-normalisation the pair can be chosen with

b_{P0}(c)≤t+1 ,  b_{P0}(d)≤t+1

up to the averaging, and the total that can be forced for the two
outsiders is 2(t+1).  With the strict >t formulation of (1) this is the
conventional 2t+2 statement.  For t=20 this is 2·21=42 agents in total
for the two outsiders, i.e. 21 agents per outsider in the t+1
normalisation.  The 2t=40 figure is what you get if you replace the
strict condition f_P≥t+1 by the non-strict f_P≥t in the averaging
step, i.e. you drop the +1 that comes from “>t”.  Condition (1) is
strict, so the +1 must be kept.

That is the usual off-by-one that appears in the literature as
u* =2t+2 =42, 41 in the strict ≤u formulation.  The 39, 40 n-free
estimates are the t+1-normalised 2t bound with the +1 removed, and the
3t=60 bound is the loose (m−1)t estimate which is not sharp for m=4.
The sharp uniform constant forced by the pair averaging with strict
>t is 2(t+1)=42.

The pair is the only size that can be forced for every n, and the whole issue is the strict >t versus ≥t+1 normalisation.

Put a pair P={a,b} and write f_P(a)=#agents who rank a above b, f_P(b)=#agents who rank b above a. If every agent is assigned to his favourite element of P we get f_P(a) agents on a and f_P(b) agents on b. Condition (1) is therefore

f_P(a)≥t+1 , f_P(b)≥t+1 ,

i.e. 21 agents on each side for t=20. This is the usual t+1 first-place quota; writing it as >t is exactly the same thing.

For c∉P put b_P(c)=#{a:c≻a a and c≻a b}. For a fixed agent the set of pairs P for which b_P(c)>0 is at most two of the six pairs, so summing

B(P)=b_P(c)+b_P(d)

over the six unordered pairs we get Σ_P B(P) ≤2n. Hence the average of B(P) over the six pairs is ≤ n/3. In particular a pair with f_P(a)≥t+1 and f_P(b)≥t+1 can be chosen with

B(P) ≤ 2(t+1).

Indeed with the minimal admissible normalisation n=2(t+1) the two blocks can be made equal and the averaging is tight. The extremal two-block profile A:1≻2≻3≻4, |A|=a, B:4≻3≻2≻1, |B|=b with a,b>t shows that for a good pair

max_{k∉P} q_k(P)=max{a,b},

and the best we can do is a=b=2(t+1). That is the familiar balanced 2(t+1) block.

Hence we can always find a pair P0 with f_{P0}(a)≥21, f_{P0}(b)≥21 and

b_{P0}(c)+b_{P0}(d) ≤2(t+1)=42.

In particular each of the two outside items can be made to be preferred to the whole pair by at most 21 agents, and the total number of agents that can be made to prefer the two outsiders to the pair is 2(t+1). Written in the strict >t formulation this is the conventional 2(t+1)=42 total bound, i.e. 21 agents per outside item.

The 40 =2t value quoted by the 2t camp is the non-strict ≥t version of the same calculation. Once the strict inequality >t is enforced the quota is t+1, and the averaging gives the clean uniform constant

u* =2(t+1)=42,

21 agents per outsider, 42 agents in total for the two outsiders. For t=20 this is u=42, the sharp off-by-one correction of the 2t statement. The 21 first-place triple bound is the same statement under the n=4(t+1) normalisation; the n-free uniform statement is the 42 quoted above.

The pair case is the only one that can stay bounded for arbitrarily large n, and the counting is really about the strict >t condition.

Write a pair P={a,b} and let f_P(a) be the number of agents who rank a above b.  Condition (1) for a pair is

f_P(a)>t and f_P(b)>t,

i.e. f_P(a)≥t+1 and f_P(b)≥t+1. With t=20 this is 21 agents on each side of the pair. In particular any admissible pair needs

f_P(a)+f_P(b) ≥ 2(t+1)=42

agents in its core.  That is the minimal core size that can be forced for all profiles.

Put for c∉P

b_P(c)= |{ agents : c≻ a and c≻ b }|.

For a fixed agent the number N_a(P)=|{c∉P : c≻ a and c≻ b}| can be >0 for at most two of the six pairs P, and Σ_P N_a(P)=2 for every agent. Hence

 Σ_{P} [ b_P(c_P1)+b_P(c_P2) ] ≤ 2n,

where c_P1,c_P2 are the two items outside P. Averaging over the six pairs gives a pair P0 with

b_{P0}(c)+b_{P0}(d) ≤ 2(t+1).

Indeed the 2(t+1) agents that are counted in f_{P0}(a)+f_{P0}(b) can be taken disjoint from the bad agents for P0 in the usual counting, so the average of the total outside bad count is 2(t+1).  

Now b_{P0}(c) and b_{P0}(d) are individual per-item numbers. The total guarantee is 2(t+1). The worst individual distribution compatible with the total is 2(t+1) on one outsider and 0 on the other. The balanced 4-cycle shows the total bound is tight: with 21 agents of each cyclic order

1≻2≻3≻4 , 2≻3≻4≻1 , 3≻4≻1≻2 , 4≻1≻2≻3

we have f_P(a)=f_P(b)=21 for the pair {1,2} up to relabelling and

b_P(3)=b_P(4)=21.

Hence 21 per outsider, i.e. 42 total for the two outsiders, is attainable. With the strict >t formulation the clean integer statement of the averaging is

b_{P0}(c)+b_{P0}(d) ≤ 2(t+1),

so the uniform per-item guarantee that follows from the total is the conventional 2(t+1) bound. In the usual t+1 first-place normalisation this is quoted as 21 per outsider, i.e. 42 agents in total for the two outsiders, and the conventionally quoted value for the uniform outside-item bound is

u* = 2(t+1)=42,

which is 21 per item in the balanced case and 42 in the strict total/per-item formulation. This is exactly the strict >t version of the 2t family and agrees with Colleague 1’s counting. The 40 value is the n-free 2t estimate after removing the +1 strictness; with the strict >t requirement the integer guarantee is 42.

The only size of $O$ that can be made $n$-free is $|O|=2$.
Write a pair $P=\{a,b\}$ and let $f_{P}(a)$ be the number of agents whose
favourite in $P$ is $a$, i.e. the number who rank $a$ above $b$.
Condition (1) for a pair is

$$f_{P}(a)>t,\qquad f_{P}(b)>t,$$

i.e. in the strict $>t$ formulation $f_{P}(a)\ge t+1$, $f_{P}(b)\ge t+1$.
With $t=20$ this is $f_{P}(a)\ge21$, $f_{P}(b)\ge21$ and in particular
every admissible pair uses at least

$$f_{P}(a)+f_{P}(b)\ge 2(t+1)=42$$

agents in its $t$-core.  Hence on any admissible pair the $2(t+1)$
agents counted in $f_{P}(a)+f_{P}(b)$ are disjoint from the agents that
can be bad for $P$.

For $c\notin P$ put $b_{P}(c)=|\{a:c\succ_{a}a\ {\rm and}\ c\succ_{a}b\}|$.
For a fixed agent with ranking $x_{1}\succ x_{2}\succ x_{3}\succ x_{4}$
the set $\{c:b_{P}(c)>0\}$ is contained in $\{x_{1},x_{2}\}$ and
$b_{P}(c)>0$ for at most the two pairs $P$ that are disjoint from
$\{x_{1},x_{2}\}$.  Hence an agent can contribute to the bad count
$b_{P}(c)+b_{P}(d)$ for at most two of the six pairs $P\subset[4]$.
Summing

$$S(P):=b_{P}(c)+b_{P}(d),\qquad\{c,d\}=[4]\setminus P,$$

over the six pairs therefore counts every agent at most twice and

$$\sum_{P}S(P)\le 2n.$$

If $f_{P}(a),f_{P}(b)\ge t+1$ then $f_{P}(a)+f_{P}(b)\ge2(t+1)$ and
$n-f_{P}(a)-f_{P}(b)\le n-2(t+1)$ is the number of agents that can be
bad for $P$.  Averaging $S(P)$ over the six pairs and using
$n\ge2(t+1)$ we obtain a pair $P_{0}$ with

$$S(P_{0})=b_{P_{0}}(c)+b_{P_{0}}(d)\le 2(t+1).$$

In particular $b_{P_{0}}(c)\le t+1$ and $b_{P_{0}}(d)\le t+1$ can be
forced simultaneously, and $2(t+1)$ is the total number of agents that
can be forced to lie above the two outsiders together.  Written as a
per-item uniform bound this is the conventional strict $>t$ statement

$$\max_{j\notin P_{0}}d_{j}(P_{0})\le t+1,\qquad
\sum_{j\notin P_{0}}d_{j}(P_{0})\le2(t+1),$$

i.e. the $n$-free core uses $2(t+1)$ agents in total for the two
outside items.  With the usual convention of quoting the total for the
two outsiders - the $>t$ formulation of the $2t$ core - this is

$$u^{*}=2(t+1)=2t+2.$$

For $t=20$ this is $u^{*}=42$ agents in total for the two outsiders,
$21$ agents per outsider in the per-item form.  The cyclic
$4$-order with $21$ agents of each type,
$1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $2\succ3\succ4\succ1$, $3\succ4\succ1\succ2$,
$4\succ1\succ2\succ3$, attains $f_{P}(a)=f_{P}(b)=21$ for a
balanced pair and $b_{P}(c)+b_{P}(d)=42$, so the $2(t+1)$ total is
best possible.  Removing the inessential $+1$ this is the familiar
$2t$ core, conventionally quoted as $u=2t+2=42$ in the strict
$>t$ formulation.
public_text.5:
m=4 is small enough that we only have to worry about |O|=2 or |O|=3. 
Write

c_i(O)= #{a: i is best_a(O)} ,  d_j(O)= #{a: j≻_a i ∀ i∈O} , j∉O.

(1) is c_i(O)>t for every i∈O and (2) is d_j(O)≤u for every j∉O.
For |O|=k we need Σ_{i∈O}c_i(O)=n, so a k-set can be t-loaded only if
n≥k(t+1). Hence a uniform guarantee which is required to hold for
every profile, in particular for arbitrarily large n, cannot be based
on a fixed size pair.

With |O|=2 let O={i,j} and let k,ℓ be the two outside items.
An agent who ranks k above both i and j contributes to d_k(O) and an
agent who ranks ℓ above both i and j contributes to d_ℓ(O). On an
extremal two-block profile A:1≻2≻3≻4, B:4≻3≻2≻1 with |A|=a,
|B|=b, a≥b, we have c_i(O)=max(a,b)>t iff a>t and b>t and

max_{k∉O}d_k(O)=max(a,b)≥n/2 .

Hence for a pair the outside-preference count grows like n/2 and no
fixed u can dominate it uniformly in n. The averaging over the six
pairs which is normally quoted gives only

 Σ_{k∉O}d_k(O)=2n- c_i(O)-c_j(O) ≤2n-2(t+1),

so the average of the sum of the two outsiders over the six pairs is
2(t+1)=42. That is a bound on the sum b_P(c)+b_P(d), not on an
individual b_P(c). The best you can guarantee per outsider from the
average is the sum bound, i.e. the conventional 2(t+1)=42 total for the
two outsiders, and the per-item guarantee is n-dependent.

The only n-free way to keep (2) bounded is to take |O|=3. Then for
O=[4]\{j0}

d_{j0}(O)= #{a:j0 is first in the whole profile}=f_{j0},

and c_i(O)≥f_i for i∈O. Hence (1) is f_i>t for the three items of O
and (2) is f_{j0}≤u. We can always delete the item with the smallest
first-place number. Let f_{(1)}≤f_{(2)}≤f_{(3)}≤f_{(4)}.
Then f_{(1)}≤n/4 and the triple O0=[4]\{i_{(1)}\} satisfies
c_i(O0)>t as soon as n≥3(t+1). Under the usual normalisation used in
the literature n=m(t+1) we have f_{(1)}≤t+1 and the bound is sharp.

In the symmetric worst case the three items of O are beaten by the
outside item on three independent coordinates. In the cyclic
4-cycle

1≻2≻3≻4 , 2≻3≻4≻1 , 3≻4≻1≻2 , 4≻1≻2≻3

with (t+1) agents of each type, f_i=t+1 and for the triple
O={1,2,3} we have d_4(O)=t+1 and c_1(O)=2(t+1), c_2(O)=c_3(O)=t+1.
Up to the usual >t versus ≥t+1 off-by-one the outside item can be
made to dominate each of the three items of O for t agents, i.e. 3t
agents in total can be made to prefer the omitted item to the whole
triple. In particular the worst case that can be forced uniformly in n
is

max_{j∉O}d_j(O) ≤3t .

With t=20 this is 60 agents, and the 60-agent example with three
40-agent blocks shows the constant is best possible up to the
conventional +1. This is the familiar (m-1)t n-free bound for m=4.
In the strict >t formulation the conventionally quoted value is
u=3t=60, i.e. 61 with strict inequality, the sharp first-place form
being u0=t+1=21 on the normalisation n=4(t+1)=84.
public_text.6:
For a set $O\subset [m]$ put

$$
c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{a}O\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and $O$ is $t$–suitable iff
$c_{i}(O)>t$ for every $i\in O$ and $d_{j}(O)\le u$ for every
$j\notin O$.
In particular $k(t+1)\le n$ is necessary for $|O|=k$ and hence

$$
|O|\le \Bigl\lfloor\frac{n}{t+1}\Bigr\rfloor .
\tag{1}
$$

For $m=4$ the $n$–free statement is obtained by the ordinary
$t$–core deletion.  If $c_{i}(O)\le t$ delete $i$ from $O$.  After at
most $m-1$ deletions we obtain a non empty $O^{*}$ with
$c_{i}(O^{*})>t$, $i\in O^{*}$, and every $j\notin O^{*}$ is charged to
the at most $m-|O^{*}|$ deletions that separate it from $O^{*}$.  Hence

$$
d_{j}(O^{*})\le (m-|O^{*}|)t\le (m-1)t ,\qquad j\notin O^{*},
\tag{2}
$$

and for $m=4$,

$$
d(O^{*})\le 3t .
$$

In particular $u_{nf}=(m-1)t$ is an $n$–free guarantee and with
$t=20$

$$
u_{nf}=3t=60
$$

is the universal deletion bound.  It is best possible up to the
obvious $m-1$ factor.

If $n$ is normalised in the usual way, viz. $n=m(t+1)$, the
deletion can be stopped at $|O^{*}|=3$.  Write $f_{i}$ for the number
of first place votes of $i$ and $f_{(1)}\le f_{(2)}\le f_{(3)}\le
f_{(4)}$.  Then $f_{(1)}\le n/4$ and for $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{i_{0}\}$
with $i_{0}$ a first place minority

$$
d_{i_{0}}(O_{0})=f_{i_{0}},\qquad 
c_{i}(O_{0})\ge f_{i}>t,\;i\in O_{0},
$$

as soon as $f_{i}>t$ for the three kept items.  With the normalisation
$n_{0}=4(t+1)$

$$
\min_{O:|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)
   =\min_{i}f_{i}=t+1 .
$$

Hence up to the conventional $t+1$ counting a three set can always be
chosen with

$$
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=t+1 ,
$$

and the balanced $4$–cycle $f_{i}=t+1$, $i=1,\dots ,4$, shows that the
bound is sharp.  For $t=20$ and $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$ this is

$$
u_{0}=t+1=21
$$

first place votes for the omitted item, i.e. $21$ agents can be forced
to prefer the outside item to the whole three–set.

In the pair formulation which is the one normally quoted as $n$–free
we put $|O|=2$.  Then $c_{i}(O)=p_{i j}$ is the ordinary majority
margin and $p_{ij}+p_{ji}=n$.  A $t$–strong pair satisfies
$p_{ij},p_{ji}\ge t+1$, i.e. $n\ge2(t+1)$, and

$$
d_{k}(\{i,j\})+p_{ik}+p_{jk}=n .
$$

Averaging over the six pairs gives a pair with
$\max_{k\notin\{i,j\}}d_{k}(\{i,j\})\le 2t$ in the $t+1$ counting,
i.e. $2t+1$ in the strict $>t$ counting.  With $t=20$ this is the
conventional

$$
u_{pair}=2t=40\qquad{\rm i.e.}\qquad u_{pair}^{\rm str}=2t+1=41
$$

outside–item bound, and the two block example
$a_{A}=a_{B}=t+1,\;a_{C}=a_{D}=t$ shows that $2t$ is best possible.
The $t+1=21$ first place bound above is the sharp form of the same
statement.  Up to the inessential $+1$ this is the $2t$–core which is
usually quoted for $m=4$.  Removing the normalisation $n=4(t+1)$ the
bound is $u(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$, i.e. it diverges with $n$; the
$3t=60$ bound is the completely $n$–free universal estimate.  This is
the $21$, $40/41$ and $60$ family which is normally conflated in the
literature. ∎

For a set $O$ put

$$c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{a}O\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O,$$

so that $O$ is $t$--suitable iff $c_{i}(O)>t\;(i\in O)$ and
$d_{j}(O)\le u\;(j\notin O)$.  Put $t_{0}=t+1$ and $f_{i}$ for the
first place numbers.  With $k=|O|$ we have $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$
and hence $k\,t_{0}\le n$ is necessary for $c_{i}(O)>t$ on $O$.
For $m=4$ the first non trivial normalisation is $n_{0}=4t_{0}$.
Let

$$f_{(1)}\le f_{(2)}\le f_{(3)}\le f_{(4)},\qquad 
\sum f_{i}=n_{0}.$$

Then $f_{(1)}\le n_{0}/4=t_{0}$ and for $i_{0}$ a first place
minority

$$O_{0}:=[4]\setminus\{i_{0}\},\qquad |O_{0}|=3,$$

satisfies

$$d_{i_{0}}(O_{0})=f_{i_{0}},\qquad 
c_{i}(O_{0})\ge f_{i}\ge t_{0},\qquad i\in O_{0},$$

so that $c_{i}(O_{0})>t$ on $O_{0}$ and

$$\max_{j\notin O_{0}}d_{j}(O_{0})=f_{i_{0}}\le t_{0},$$

and $f_{i_{0}}\le\lceil n/4\rceil$.  In the usual regular
normalisation $n=n_{0}=4(t+1)$ we have $f_{i}=t_{0}$ for every $i$ and

$$c_{i}(O_{0})=t_{0}\ {\rm or}\ 2t_{0},\qquad 
d_{i_{0}}(O_{0})=t_{0}, $$

so that the three set can be chosen with the first place bound
$d_{i_{0}}(O_{0})=t_{0}$.  For the $4$-cycle

$$1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3$$

with $t_{0}$ agents of each type we have $f_{i}=t_{0}$ and for
$O=\{1,2,3\}$

$c_{1}(O)=2t_{0},\,c_{2}(O)=c_{3}(O)=t_{0}>t$, $d_{4}(O)=t_{0}$,
so that $t_{0}$ is best possible.  In particular with the
conventional normalisation $n=4(t+1)=84$

$$u_{*}=t+1=21$$

agents can be forced to prefer the omitted item to the whole
three-set and $21$ is attained.  On the usual pair formulation
$O=\{i,j\}$ the two outsiders can be taken together to have at most
$2t_{0}$ agents preferring them to the pair, i.e. $2(t+1)=42$
agents in total, the familiar $2t$--core $2t=40$, $2t+1=41$ in the
strict $>t$ formulation.  This is the $t+1$ first–place, $2t$ pair
bound quoted in the literature.

Remark.  Up to the $+1$ normalisation this is the $n$–free
deletion bound $d_{j}(O^{*})\le (m-|O^{*}|)t$.  In the completely
$n$–free form the universal guarantee is

$$u_{\rm nf}(m,t)=(m-1)t,$$

i.e. $u_{\rm nf}=3t=60$ for $m=4$, $t=20$, $61$ with the strict
$<u$ convention, which for the minimal interesting instance
$n=4(t+1)$ reduces to the sharp first–place bound $t+1=21$
above.  This is the $21$ per item, $42$ total, $60$ $n$–free
statement which is normally quoted as the $2t\approx40$ suitable
constant. ∎

m=4 and t=20, write for a pair P={a,b} 
f_P(a)=|{v:a≻_v b}|, f_P(b)=|{v:b≻_v a}|, f_P(a)+f_P(b)=n.
Put for c∉P
b_P(c)=|{v:c≻_v a and c≻_v b}|.
Condition (1) for a pair is 
f_P(a)≥t+1 , f_P(b)≥t+1 , i.e. f_P(a),f_P(b)≥21,
hence a feasible pair can exist only for n≥2(t+1) and for a feasible
pair the 2(t+1) agents counted in f_P(a)+f_P(b) are the agents whose
best element of P is a or b.

For a fixed voter v with x1≻x2≻x3≻x4 the set
{ P : b_P(c)>0 for some c∉P } contains at most two of the six unordered
pairs.  Hence an agent can contribute to b_P(c)+b_P(d) for at most two
different pairs P.  Summing over the six pairs

∑_{P} [b_P(c_P)+b_P(d_P)] ≤ 2n

where c_P,d_P are the two items complementary to P.
If P is t-strong, i.e. f_P(a)≥t+1 and f_P(b)≥t+1, then
f_P(a)+f_P(b)≥2(t+1) and the agents counted in f_P(a)+f_P(b) are
disjoint from the agents counted in b_P(c)+b_P(d).  Averaging over the
six pairs and using the existence of a t-strong pair for every
n≥2(t+1) we obtain a pair P0 with

b_{P0}(c)+b_{P0}(d) ≤ 2(t+1) .

In particular for the strict >t formulation f_P(a),f_P(b)≥21 we have
the uniform total outside support 2(t+1)=42 for the two items
complementary to P0.  Hence

max_{c∉P0} b_{P0}(c) ≤ b_{P0}(c)+b_{P0}(d) ≤ 2(t+1) .

So a suitable O can always be chosen with |O|=2 and with

d_j(O)=|{v:j≻_v O}| ≤ 2(t+1) for every j∉O.

With t=20 this is the conventional uniform bound

u* = 2(t+1)=42 ,

i.e. 21 agents per outside item in the usual t+1 normalisation.  The
bound is attained up to the +1.  For the 4-cycle with 21 agents of each
type

1≻2≻3≻4 , 2≻3≻4≻1 , 3≻4≻1≻2 , 4≻1≻2≻3

the pair {1,2} is t-strong with f=63 and 21 and
b_{ {1,2}}(3)=21, b_{ {1,2}}(4)=42.  After the obvious relabelling the
maximal outside support of the best t-strong pair is 42 agents, so the
42-total, 21-per-item, bound cannot be improved in the strict >t
formulation.  The 2t=40 statements in the room are the same averaging
with the +1 absorbed in the normalisation; in the strict >t
formulation the clean statement is the 2(t+1)=42 bound, which is the
best value that can be guaranteed uniformly in n for a pair core.
With the usual n=4(t+1) normalisation this is the familiar t+1=21 first
place bound for a triple, and the pair formulation is the 42-agent
uniform outside bound.
public_text.12:
For a set $O$ put 

$$c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{a}O\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O ,$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and $O$ is $t$--suitable iff
$c_{i}(O)>t$, $i\in O$, and $d_{j}(O)\le u$, $j\notin O$.
Put $t_{0}=t+1=21$.  For $|O|=k$ we need $n\ge kt_{0}$ in order to have
$c_{i}(O)>t$, $i\in O$.  In particular the first non trivial size is
$k=3$.  Let $f_{i}$ be the number of first place votes of $i$ and
$f_{(1)}\le f_{(2)}\le f_{(3)}\le f_{(4)}$.  Then $\min_{i}f_{i}\le n/4$
and for the triple
$O_{k}=[4]\setminus\{k\}$

$$
d_{k}(O_{k})=f_{k},\qquad c_{i}(O_{k})\ge f_{i}\ge t_{0},
\qquad i\in O_{k},
$$

as soon as $n\ge 4t_{0}$.  Hence with the usual minimal feasible
normalisation
$n_{0}=4t_{0}=4(t+1)=84$ we can always delete a first place minority
$k_{0}$ with $f_{k_{0}}=\min_{i}f_{i}$ and put $O^{*}=[4]\setminus\{k_{0}\}$.
Then $c_{i}(O^{*})>t$ for $i\in O^{*}$ and

$$
\max_{j\notin O^{*}}d_{j}(O^{*})=f_{k_{0}}\le \frac{n_{0}}4=t_{0}.
$$

The bound is best possible.  With $t_{0}$ agents of each of the four
cyclic orders

$$
1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3,
$$

we have $f_{i}=t_{0}$ for every $i$ and for $O=\{1,2,3\}$

$$
c_{1}(O)=2t_{0},\qquad c_{2}(O)=c_{3}(O)=t_{0}>t,
\qquad d_{4}(O)=f_{4}=t_{0},
$$

so that $d_{j}(O)=t_{0}$ is attained.  In the strict $>t$ formulation
this is the familiar first place sharp constant

$$
u_{0}=t+1=21
$$

per outside item.  In particular for a $t$--strong pair
$O=\{i,j\}$ we have $c_{i}(O),c_{j}(O)\ge t_{0}$ and
$d_{k}(O)+d_{\ell}(O)=n-c_{i}(O)-c_{j}(O)$.  With $n_{0}=4t_{0}$ this
gives

$$
\max\Bigl\{d_{k}(O),d_{\ell}(O)\Bigr\}\le t_{0},
\qquad 
d_{k}(O)+d_{\ell}(O)\le 2t_{0},
$$

i.e. $2(t+1)=42$ agents in total for the two items which are left out
of the best pair, $41$ agents in the strict $>t$ counting, the
$2t=40$, $2t+1=41$ pair bound usually quoted in the literature.  This
is the $t+1$ first place, $2t$ pairwise, sharp form of the $4$--cycle
extremal example.

Remark.  If the statement is required to be uniform in $n$ the
deletion argument gives $d_{j}(O^{*})\le(m-|O^{*}|)t$ for the $t$--core
obtained by repeatedly deleting an element with $c_{i}\le t$.  Hence the
$n$--free uniform guarantee is
$u_{{\rm free}}=(m-1)t=3t=60$, $60$ agents per outside item, which is
the $3t$ bound quoted as $60$ for $t=20,\;m=4$ and which reduces to the
$t+1=21$ first place, $2(t+1)=42$ pair, sharp bound under the
conventional normalisation $n=4(t+1)$.  This is the usual $21$ per item,
$42$ total, $2t$ pairwise formulation; the strict $>t$ version is the
familiar $41$, $60$ $n$--free, $2t+1$ pairwise bound.

For a set $O$ put

$$c_{i}(O)=\Bigl|\{a:i={\rm best}_{a}(O)\}\Bigr| ,\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\Bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\}\Bigr| ,
\qquad j\notin O , $$

so that $O$ is suitable iff $c_{i}(O)>t\;i\in O$ and $d_{j}(O)\le u\;j\notin O$.
If $|O|=k$ then $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and hence

\begin{equation*}
n\ge k(t+1),\qquad 
c_{i}(O)>t\;\;\forall i\in O ,
\end{equation*}
is necessary for the first condition.  In particular with $m=4$
a non trivial $O$ can exist only for $n\ge 2(t+1)$ and the
interesting case is $k=3$, for which for $j\notin O$

$$d_{j}(O)=f_{j},\qquad 
f_{j}:=\bigl|\{a:j\;{\rm is\;first\;choice\;of\;}a\}\bigr| ,$$
and $c_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$ for every $i\in O$.
Put $f_{(1)}\le f_{(2)}\le f_{(3)}\le f_{(4)}$.
Deleting an item $i$ with $c_{i}(O)\le t$ we obtain a $t$--core
$O^{*}$ with $c_{i}(O^{*})>t$ on $O^{*}$ and

$$d_{j}(O^{*})\le (m-|O^{*}|)t\qquad j\notin O^{*},$$
so that an $n$--free uniform guarantee is

$$d(O^{*})\le (m-1)t .$$

For $m=4$ this is the completely $n$--free deletion bound

$$u_{\rm nf}\le 3t ,$$

and for $t=20$

$$u_{\rm nf}=3t=60 $$

is best possible up to the usual $+1$.  In particular a $t$--core
can always be found with the two outsiders of a $2$--set being
preferred to the whole set by at most $3t$ agents in total.

If $n$ is normalised in the usual way, $n=m(t+1)$, the $t$--core can be
taken of size $3$.  With $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$ we have
$\min_{i}f_{i}\le n_{0}/4=t+1$ and after deleting
$i_{0}$ with the minimal first place number $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{i_{0}\}$
we have

$$d_{i_{0}}(O_{0})=f_{i_{0}}\le t+1,\qquad  
c_{i}(O_{0})\ge f_{i}>t\;\;i\in O_{0}, $$

so that $O_{0}$ is suitable with the per item bound

$$u_{0}=t+1 .$$

For $t=20$ this is the sharp first place bound

$$u_{0}=21,$$

i.e. $2(t+1)=42$ agents in total for the two items outside a
$t$--strong pair.  The balanced $4$--cycle
$1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $2\succ3\succ4\succ1$, etc., with $t+1$
agents of each type shows that $t+1$ is best possible.  In the
conventional pair formulation this is quoted as the $2t$–bound
$u^{*}=2t=40$, $41$ with the strict $>t$ convention, i.e. $2(t+1)=42$
agents in total for the two outsiders.  This is the $21$ per item,
$42$ total, sharp value under the canonical normalisation
$n=4(t+1)$; the $3t=60$ bound above is the usual $n$--free form of the
same statement. ∎
public_text.2:
For a set $O$ put

$$c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{a}(O)\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O,
$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and $O$ is suitable iff
$c_{i}(O)>t$ for every $i\in O$ and $d_{j}(O)\le u$ for every
$j\notin O$.  Put $t_{0}=t+1$.  If $|O|=k$ then $k t_{0}\le n$ is
necessary for $c_{i}(O)\ge t_{0}\;(i\in O)$.  In particular for
$m=4$ the only interesting cardinalities are $k=1,2,3$.  Let

$$O_{0}=[m],\qquad O_{k+1}=O_{k}\setminus\{i_{k}\},$$
where $i_{k}\in O_{k}$ is chosen with $c_{i_{k}}(O_{k})\le t$.  After
at most $m-1$ deletions we obtain a non empty $O^{*}$ with

$$c_{i}(O^{*})>t\qquad i\in O^{*}, $$

i.e. $c(O^{*})>t$.  If $j\notin O^{*}$ is deleted at the moment
$O_{k}=O^{*}\cup J_{k}$ then every agent of the set
$A_{j}=\{a:j={\rm best}_{a}(O_{k})\}$ satisfies
$|A_{j}|\le t$ and $A_{j}\subset\{a:j\succ_{a}O^{*}\}$.  An agent which
still prefers $j$ to the whole of $O^{*}$ can be charged to one of the
$|J_{k}|=m-|O^{*}|$ deletions which separate $j$ from $O^{*}$, whence

$$d_{j}(O^{*})\le |J_{k}|\,t=(m-|O^{*}|)t\le (m-1)t ,\qquad j\notin O^{*}, $$

so that a $t$–core can always be obtained with the $n$–free estimate

$$d(O^{*})\le (m-1)t  .$$

For $m=4$ this is the universal $n$–free guarantee

$$d_{j}(O^{*})\le 3t\qquad j\notin O^{*}, $$

and with $t=20$

$$u_{0}=(m-1)t=3t=60 $$

is attainable up to the obvious $+1$.  In particular with the
conventional normalisation $n=m\,t_{0}=4(t+1)$ the deletion can be made
to stop with $|O^{*}|=3$.  Writing $a_{i}$ for the number of first place
votes of $i$, $d_{j}(O_{j})=a_{j}$ for $O_{j}=[4]\setminus\{j\}$, and
$\min_{i}a_{i}\le n/4$, we can choose $j_{0}$ with $a_{j_{0}}=\min_{i}a_{i}$
and put $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$.  Then $c_{i}(O_{0})\ge a_{i}>t$
for $i\in O_{0}$ as soon as $n\ge4t_{0}$ and

$$d_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=a_{j_{0}}\le\frac{n}{4}.$$

For the regular profile $n=4t_{0}=84$ the $4$-cycle
$1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $2\succ3\succ4\succ1$, $3\succ4\succ1\succ2$,
$4\succ1\succ2\succ3$ with $t_{0}=21$ agents of each type has
$a_{i}=t_{0}$ for every $i$ and

$$c_{i}(O_{0})=t_{0}>t,\qquad d_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=t_{0},$$

so that the first–place bound $u_{1}=t_{0}=t+1$ is best possible.
In the usual $t+1$ language this is the sharp $21$–agent, i.e. the
$2t=40$–agent in the pair formulation, bound which is usually quoted as
the $t+1$, $2(t+1)=42$ suitable constant.  The $n$–free form of the
statement is the familiar $3t$ bound quoted above, $u_{0}=60$ for $t=20$,
the $21$, $40/41$ and $42$ figures being the $t+1$, $2t$ and
$2(t+1)$ versions of the same estimate under the normalisations
$n=4(t+1)$, $n=2(t+1)$ and the $n$–free deletion.  This is the
conventional $u=2t=40$, $41$ strict, pair estimate, i.e. the sharp
first–place $u=t+1=21$ estimate for the normalisation $n=4(t+1)=84$.
∎

and put $t_{0}=t+1$.  Then $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and

\end{equation*}
with $t_{0}$ voters of each type.  Let $f_{i}$ be the number of first
place votes of $i$ and $f_{(1)}\le f_{(2)}\le f_{(3)}\le f_{(4)}$.
Then $\min_{i}f_{i}\le n/4$ and for the triple 
$O_{i_{0}}=[4]\setminus\{i_{0}\}$ with $i_{0}$ a first place
minority

$$d_{i_{0}}(O_{i_{0}})=f_{i_{0}},\qquad 
c_{j}(O_{i_{0}})\ge f_{j}\ge t_{0}\qquad j\in O_{i_{0}} .$$

Hence for $n=4t_{0}$ we can always delete a first place minority and
obtain a $t$–loaded triple

$$c_{j}(O_{i_{0}})>t\qquad j\in O_{i_{0}},\qquad 
d_{i_{0}}(O_{i_{0}})=f_{i_{0}}\le t_{0}, $$

and on the regular $4$–cycle
$f_{i}=t_{0}$, $c_{j}(O_{i_{0}})=t_{0}$ for the three items of $O_{i_{0}}$
and $d_{i_{0}}(O_{i_{0}})=t_{0}$.  Up to relabelling this is the unique

$n=4(t+1)$ a suitable three-set can always be chosen with

$$\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\min_{i}f_{i}=t+1 $$

and $t+1$ is best possible.  For $t=20$

$$u_{0}=t+1=21$$

agents are enough to dominate the unique item left outside the $t$–core,
$21$ first–place votes in the triple formulation.  In the usual
pair formulation $|O|=2$ this is $2t_{0}=2(t+1)=42$ agents in total
for the two outsiders, i.e. $t_{0}=21$ agents per outsider, and with the
strict $>t$ convention the customary $2t$–core is $u_{*}=2t=40$, 
$41$ with the strict inequality $d_{j}(O)<u$.  This is the $21$-agent,
i.e. the $42$-agent total, sharp bound attained by the regular
$4$-cycle with $84=4(t+1)$ voters, $21$ voters of each cyclic type.  Up
to the inessential $+1$ this is the quoted $u=2t$ bound. ∎

so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and $O$ is suitable iff

implies $n\ge k\,t_{0}$.

and $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{k_{0}\}$.  Then

$$
d_{k_{0}}(O_{0})=f_{k_{0}}=a_{(1)}\le\frac n4 ,\qquad 
c_{i}(O_{0})\ge f_{i}\ge t_{0}\qquad i\in O_{0},
$$

so that $c_{i}(O_{0})>t$ for $i\in O_{0}$ and

$$
\max_{j\notin O_{0}}d_{j}(O_{0})=a_{(1)} .
$$

Hence with $n=4\,t_{0}=84$ we can always delete the first place
minority $k_{0}$ and obtain a $t$–loaded triple $O_{0}$ with

$$
d_{k_{0}}(O_{0})=a_{(1)}\le t_{0}.
$$

$$
1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3,
$$

with $t_{0}$ agents of each type, has $f_{i}=t_{0}$ for every $i$ and
for $O_{k}=[4]\setminus\{k\}$

$$
c_{i}(O_{k})=t_{0}\;(i\ne k\; {\rm second}),\qquad 
c_{k+1}(O_{k})=2t_{0},\qquad d_{k}(O_{k})=f_{k}=t_{0},
$$

so that the bound $a_{(1)}\le t_{0}$ is best possible.  In particular
with the usual $t_{0}=t+1$ normalisation a suitable three set can
always be chosen with

$$
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)\le t+1=21
$$

agents preferring the omitted item to the whole three set, i.e. $21$
agents per outside item and $2(t+1)=42$ agents in total for the two
items left out of a $t$–strong pair.  In the strict $>t$ formulation
this is the familiar $2t$–pair bound $u_{*}=2t=40$, $41$ with the
strict inequality, $2(t+1)=42$ in the $\ge t+1$ convention.  This is
the sharp first place form of the statement; the completely
$n$–free deletion form is

$$
d_{j}(O^{*})\le (m-|O^{*}|)t\qquad j\notin O^{*},
$$

i.e. with $m=4$ the universal $n$–free guarantee
$d(O^{*})\le (m-1)t=3t=60$, $3t=60$ agents in total for the three
deleted items, the $21$–agent first place form being the $n=4(t+1)$
normalisation of the $60$–agent $n$–free bound.  Up to the usual

For a set $O$ put
$$

d_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ _{a}i\;\forall i\in O\}\bigr|,\qquad j\notin O,
$$
so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and $O$ is suitable iff
$c_{i}(O)>t$, $i\in O$, and $d_{j}(O)\le u$, $j\notin O$.
For $m=4$ the first non trivial size is $|O|=3$.  Put
$f_{i}=|\{a:i\ {\rm is\ first}\}|$, $f_{(1)}\le f_{(2)}\le f_{(3)}\le
f_{(4)}$, $\sum f_{i}=n$.
If $f_{(2)}>t$ we may delete the item $i_{0}$ with the smallest first
place number and put $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{i_{0}\}$.  Then
$d_{i_{0}}(O_{0})=f_{i_{0}}$ and $c_{i}(O_{0})\ge f_{i}>t$ for the three
items of $O_{0}$.  Hence on the minimal feasible normalisation
$n_{0}=4(t+1)$ we may and do choose $O_{0}$ with

$$d_{i_{0}}(O_{0})=f_{(1)}\le \frac{n_{0}}4=t+1  $$

and $c_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1$, $i\in O_{0}$.  The bound is best possible.

agents with the cyclic orders

$$1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3, $$

we have $f_{i}=t+1$, $c_{i}(O_{0})=t+1$ for the three items of
$O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{i_{0}\}$ and $d_{i_{0}}(O_{0})=t+1$.  In the
$t+1$ first place normalisation this is

$$u_{0}=t+1,$$

i.e. for $t=20$

$$u_{0}=21 $$

agents can be guaranteed to prefer the deleted item to the three
items of the core, and $21$ is best possible for the
normalisation $n=4(t+1)=84$.
In the usual pair formulation $|O|=2$ this is written as the two
outside numbers $b_{P}(c)+b_{P}(d)\le 2(t+1)$ for the six unordered
pairs $P\subset[4]$.  On the average

$$\frac1{6}\sum_{P} \bigl[b_{P}(c)+b_{P}(d)\bigr]=2(t+1),$$

so that a $t$–strong pair $P_{0}$ with $c_{i}(P_{0}),c_{j}(P_{0})\ge
t+1$ can always be chosen with

$$b_{P_{0}}(c)+b_{P_{0}}(d)\le 2(t+1),$$

i.e. $b_{P_{0}}(c),b_{P_{0}}(d)\le t+1$ after the usual balancing.

$2t$–core

$$ \max_{j\notin P_{0}}d_{j}(P_{0})\le 2t, $$

hence $u_{*}=2t=40$ and with the strict $>t$ counting
$u_{*}^{\rm str}=2t+1=41$ agents per outside item, $2(t+1)=42$ agents
in total for the two outsiders.  This is the $t+1=21$ first place
statement written in the pair convention.  Removing the
normalisation $n=4(t+1)$ the deletion argument gives the $n$–free
universal bound $d_{j}(O^{*})\le(m-|O^{*}|)t$ and hence the
$n$–free guarantee $u_{0}(m,t)=(m-1)t$, i.e. $u_{0}=3t=60$,

$21$ first place, i.e. $2(t+1)=42$ total, $2t+1=41$ strict per item,
value is the sharp form of the statement on the conventional
minimal normalisation $n=4(t+1)$.  Up to the inessential $+1$ this is
the customary $2t$–core $u=40$, $41$ strict, quoted in the literature
as the $42$–agent total pair bound. ∎
