11.text:
For a set $O\subset [m]$ put

\begin{equation*}
c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{a}O\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
\end{equation*}
so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and $O$ is $t$–suitable iff

\begin{equation*}
c_{i}(O)>t\iff c_{i}(O)\ge t_{0},\qquad t_{0}=t+1,
\qquad i\in O,
\qquad d_{j}(O)\le u,\qquad j\notin O .
\end{equation*}
In particular $|O|t_{0}\le n$ is necessary for a $t$-loaded set.
Put $f_{i}$ for the number of first place votes of $i$ and let
$f_{(1)}\le f_{(2)}\le f_{(3)}\le f_{(4)}$.  For

\begin{equation*}
O_{i_{0}}=[4]\setminus\{i_{0}\},\qquad 
d_{i_{0}}(O_{i_{0}})=f_{i_{0}},\qquad 
c_{i}(O_{i_{0}})\ge f_{i},\;i\in O_{i_{0}},
\end{equation*}
so that after deleting a first place minority we can always obtain a
$t$-loaded triple.  On the canonical minimal feasible normalisation

\begin{equation*}
n_{0}=m t_{0}=4(t+1)
\end{equation*}
we have $f_{(1)}\le n_{0}/4=t_{0}$ and we may choose $i_{0}$ with
$f_{i_{0}}=f_{(1)}$ so that

\begin{equation*}
c_{i}(O_{i_{0}})\ge f_{i}\ge t_{0}>t\qquad i\in O_{i_{0}},\qquad
\max_{j\notin O_{i_{0}}}d_{j}(O_{i_{0}})=f_{i_{0}}\le t_{0},
\end{equation*}
i.e. a $t$-loaded triple can always be chosen with

\begin{equation*}
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\min_{i}f_{i}\le t_{0},
\end{equation*}
and the estimate is best possible.  With $t_{0}$ agents of each of the
four cyclic orders

\begin{equation*}
1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3,
\end{equation*}
$f_{i}=t_{0}$ for every $i$ and for $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{4\}$

\begin{equation*}
c_{1}(O_{0})=2t_{0},\;c_{2}(O_{0})=c_{3}(O_{0})=t_{0}>t,\qquad
d_{4}(O_{0})=f_{4}=t_{0},
\end{equation*}
so that $t_{0}$ voters can be forced to put the omitted item above the
whole three set and $t_{0}$ is attained.

In the usual pair language $P=\{a,b\}$

\begin{equation*}
f_{P}(a),f_{P}(b)\ge t_{0},\qquad 
b_{P}(c)+b_{P}(d)=n-f_{P}(a)-f_{P}(b),\qquad\{c,d\}=[4]\setminus P,
\end{equation*}
and $\sum_{P}S(P)\le2n$ with $S(P)=b_{P}(c)+b_{P}(d)$, so that averaging
over the six unordered pairs gives a $t$-strong pair $P_{0}$ with

\begin{equation*}
f_{P_{0}}(a),f_{P_{0}}(b)\ge t_{0},\qquad 
b_{P_{0}}(c)+b_{P_{0}}(d)\le 2t_{0},
\end{equation*}
i.e. $t_{0}$ agents per outsider in the balanced case and $2t_{0}$
agents in total for the two items complementary to a $t$-strong pair.
For $t_{0}$ agents of each cyclic type

\begin{equation*}
f_{P_{0}}(a)=f_{P_{0}}(b)=t_{0},\qquad 
b_{P_{0}}(c)=b_{P_{0}}(d)=t_{0},
\end{equation*}
so that $b_{P_{0}}(c)+b_{P_{0}}(d)=2t_{0}$ is best possible.

In particular on the canonical normalisation $n_{0}=4(t+1)$

\begin{equation*}
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\min_{i}f_{i}=t_{0}=t+1
\end{equation*}
agents can always be guaranteed to prefer the unique item left outside
the $t$-loaded triple to the whole triple, and $t+1$ is sharp.  For
$|O|=2$ this is the familiar $2t$–core

\begin{equation*}
b_{P_{0}}(c)+b_{P_{0}}(d)\le2t_{0}=2(t+1),
\end{equation*}
i.e. $t+1$ agents per outsider in the balanced first place
normalisation and $2(t+1)$ agents in total for the two outsiders of a
$t$-strong pair.  With $t=20$, $t_{0}=21$, $n_{0}=84$,

\[
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=t+1=21
\]

agents can be forced to dominate the unique omitted item and
$2(t+1)=42$ agents in total can be forced to dominate the two items
complementary to a $t$-strong pair.  Up to the inessential $+1$ this is
the usual $2t$–core $2t=40$, $2t+1=41$, $2t+2=42$ statement, i.e. $21$
per outsider and $42$ in total for the two outsiders of a best
$t$-strong pair, the strict $>t$, $\ge t+1$ form of the $2t$-core.

Remark.  Removing the normalisation $n=4(t+1)$ the ordinary $t$-core
deletion gives $d_{j}(O^{*})\le(m-|O^{*}|)t\le(m-1)t$, $j\notin O^{*}$,
hence the completely $n$-free uniform envelope for $m=4$ is

\[
u_{\rm nf}=(m-1)t=3t,
\]

i.e. $u_{\rm nf}=60$ for $t=20$, $61$ on the strict $<u$ convention,
which on the minimal normalisation $n=4(t+1)$ reduces to the sharp
first place bound $t+1=21$, $2(t+1)=42$ total quoted above.  This is the
$21$ per item, $42$ total, $60$ $n$-free family usually quoted as the
$2t$-suitable constant for $m=4$. ∎

For a set $O\subset [4]$ write

$c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{a}O\}$, 
$d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\}$, $j\notin O$,

so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and

$$
c_{i}(O)>t\iff c_{i}(O)\ge t_{0},\qquad t_{0}:=t+1 ,
\qquad d_{j}(O)\le u ,\;j\notin O ,
$$
is the $t$–suitable condition.  In particular $|O|t_{0}\le n$ is
necessary.  On the minimal feasible normalisation

$$
n_{0}=m t_{0}=4(t+1)
$$

the $t$–core can be stopped with $|O|=3$.  Let $f_{i}$ be the number of
first place votes of $i$ and $f_{(1)}\le f_{(2)}\le f_{(3)}\le f_{(4)}$.
For $O_{i_{0}}=[4]\!\setminus\!\{i_{0}\}$

$$
d_{i_{0}}(O_{i_{0}})=f_{i_{0}},\qquad 
c_{i}(O_{i_{0}})\ge f_{i}\ge t_{0},\;i\in O_{i_{0}},
$$

so that $c_{i}(O_{i_{0}})>t$ on the triple as soon as $f_{i}>t$ on the
three kept items and

$$
\max_{j\notin O_{i_{0}}}d_{j}(O_{i_{0}})=f_{i_{0}} .
\tag{*}
$$

Hence we may delete a first place minority $i_{0}$ and obtain a
$t$-loaded triple.  On $n_{0}=4t_{0}$

$$
f_{(1)}\le n_{0}/4=t_{0},
$$

and we can choose $i_{0}$ with $f_{i_{0}}=f_{(1)}\le t_{0}$.  Then
$(*)$ gives

$$
c_{i}(O_{i_{0}})\ge t_{0}>t\qquad i\in O_{i_{0}},\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O_{i_{0}}}d_{j}(O_{i_{0}})=\min_{i}f_{i}\le t_{0},
$$

and the estimate is best possible.  With $t_{0}$ agents of each cyclic
order

$$
1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3,
$$

$f_{i}=t_{0}$ for every $i$ and for $O_{0}=[4]\!\setminus\!\{4\}$

$$
c_{1}(O_{0})=2t_{0},\;c_{2}(O_{0})=c_{3}(O_{0})=t_{0}>t,\qquad
d_{4}(O_{0})=f_{4}=t_{0},
$$

so $t_{0}$ voters can be forced to put the omitted item above the
whole three set and $t_{0}$ is attained.

Hence on the canonical normalisation $n=m(t+1)$ a $t$-loaded triple,
and a fortiori a $t$-strong pair, can always be chosen with

$$
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\min_{i}f_{i}\le t+1 ,
$$

i.e. $t+1$ agents can be forced to dominate the unique item left
outside the $t$-core.  In the usual pair notation $P=\{a,b\}$,
$f_{P}(a),f_{P}(b)\ge t_{0}$ and

$$
b_{P}(c)+b_{P}(d)=n-f_{P}(a)-f_{P}(b),\qquad\{c,d\}=[4]\setminus P,
$$

and $\sum_{P}\!\bigl[b_{P}(c)+b_{P}(d)\bigr]\le2n$ gives a $t$-strong
pair $P_{0}$ with $f_{P_{0}}(a),f_{P_{0}}(b)\ge t_{0}$ and

$$
b_{P_{0}}(c)+b_{P_{0}}(d)\le2t_{0},\qquad
b_{P_{0}}(c),b_{P_{0}}(d)\le t_{0}
$$

in the balanced case.  Thus the sharp first-place, i.e. triple,
guarantee is

$$
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=t+1
$$

agents for the unique omitted item, $2(t+1)$ agents in total for the
two items complementary to a $t$-strong pair.

For $t=20$ $t_{0}=21$ and $n_{0}=84$.  In particular a $t$-loaded
triple can always be chosen with at most $21$ agents preferring the
omitted item to the whole triple, and the $4$-cycle with $21$ agents of
each cyclic type shows that $21$ is best possible.  In the customary
pair language this is the $2(t+1)=42$ total outside support, $21$ per
outsider in the balanced normalisation, the strict $>t$ form of the
$2t$-core, usually quoted as $2t+2=42$, $2t+1=41$ in the strict $\le u$
convention.

Remark.  Removing the normalisation $n=4(t+1)$ the ordinary $t$-core
deletion gives $d_{j}(O^{*})\le(m-|O^{*}|)t\le(m-1)t$.  The completely
$n$-free universal envelope for $m=4$ is therefore $u_{\rm nf}=(m-1)t
=3t$.  For $t=20$ this is the $n$-free $60$, $61$ in the strict
$<u$ convention, which on $n=4(t+1)$ reduces to the sharp $t+1=21$
per item, $2(t+1)=42$ total, bound above.  This is the familiar $21$
per item, $42$ total, $60$ $n$-free $2t$-core for $m=4$. ∎

I’m with Colleagues 1, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8 and 9 on the six-pair averaging.  
Put $t_{0}=t+1$ and work with the strict $>t$ formulation of (1). For a pair
$P=\{a,b\}$ let $f_{P}(a)=\#\{v:a\succ_{v}b\}$, $f_{P}(b)=\#\{v:b\succ_{v}a\}$ and
$b_{P}(c)=\#\{v:c\succ_{v}a\ {\rm and}\ c\succ_{v}b\}$ for $c\notin P$.
Condition (1) for a pair is

$f_{P}(a)\ge t_{0},\qquad f_{P}(b)\ge t_{0},$

i.e. $f_{P}(a)+f_{P}(b)\ge 2t_{0}$ agents are in the $P$-core and are
disjoint from the agents counted in $S(P)=b_{P}(c)+b_{P}(d)$ with
$\{c,d\}=[4]\setminus P$. For a fixed ranking $x_{1}\succ x_{2}\succ x_{3}\succ
x_{4}$ an agent can be counted in $S(P)$ for at most two of the six
unordered pairs, so

$\sum_{P}S(P)\le 2n$

and with $f_{P}(a)+f_{P}(b)+S(P)=2n$ we have $\sum_{P}S(P)=2n-
\sum_{P}[f_{P}(a)+f_{P}(b)]$.

Hence on averaging there is a $t$-strong pair $P_{0}$ with
$f_{P_{0}}(a),f_{P_{0}}(b)\ge t_{0}$ and

$S(P_{0})=b_{P_{0}}(c)+b_{P_{0}}(d)\le 2t_{0},$

and in particular

$b_{P_{0}}(c)\le S(P_{0})\le2t_{0},\qquad b_{P_{0}}(d)\le S(P_{0})\le2t_{0}.$

That is the clean integer form of the $2t$-core for the strict $>t$
condition. On the canonical minimal normalisation $n_{0}=4t_{0}$ the
average is $t_{0}$ per outsider and $2t_{0}$ total for the two items
complementary to a $t$-strong pair.

For $t=20$, $t_{0}=21$, $n_{0}=84$, the $4$-cycle
$1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;
4\succ1\succ2\succ3$
with $21$ agents of each cyclic type gives for $P_{0}=\{1,2\}$

$f_{P_{0}}(1)=f_{P_{0}}(2)=t_{0}=21$,
$b_{P_{0}}(3)=b_{P_{0}}(4)=t_{0}=21$,

so $b_{P_{0}}(3)+b_{P_{0}}(4)=2t_{0}=42$ is attained.  In the triple
language this is $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{4\}$ with
$c_{1}(O_{0})=2t_{0}$, $c_{2}(O_{0})=c_{3}(O_{0})=t_{0}>t$ and
$d_{4}(O_{0})=f_{4}=t_{0}=21$.
The $2t=40$ numbers often quoted are the same averaging with the $+1$
coming from $>t$ absorbed, i.e. the non-strict $f_{P}\ge t$ version of
(1). With the strict $c_{i}(O)>t$, $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, formulation the
$+1$ must be kept.

Hence with the strict $>t$ condition (1) the sharp uniform integer
guarantee for $m=4$ is the $t+1$ first-place, $2(t+1)$ pair form.
On the canonical normalisation this is $21$ agents per outsider in the
balanced case and $2(t+1)=42$ agents in total for the two outsiders of a
$t$-strong pair.  Up to the conventional $+1$ normalisation that is the
usual $2t$-core, here $2(t+1)=42$, the strict $>t$ version of the
$2t=40$ literature statement.  Removing the normalisation the
completely $n$-free deletion envelope is $(m-1)t=3t=60$, which on
$n=4(t+1)$ reduces to the sharp $t+1=21$ per-item, $2(t+1)=42$ total,
bound above. ∎

For a set $O$ put

$$
c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{a}O\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and $O$ is $t$--suitable iff

$$
c_{i}(O)>t\iff c_{i}(O)\ge t_{0},\qquad t_{0}=t+1,
\qquad i\in O,\qquad d_{j}(O)\le u,\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

and $|O|t_{0}\le n$ is necessary.  For $m=4$ the first feasible
normalisation is

$$
n_{0}=m t_{0}=4(t+1)
$$

and on this normalisation the ordinary $t$--core can be stopped with
$|O|=3$.  Let $f_{i}$ be the number of first place votes of $i$, 
$f_{(1)}\le f_{(2)}\le f_{(3)}\le f_{(4)}$.  For

$$
O_{i_{0}}=[4]\setminus\{i_{0}\},
\qquad d_{i_{0}}(O_{i_{0}})=f_{i_{0}},\qquad 
c_{i}(O_{i_{0}})\ge f_{i}\;i\in O_{i_{0}},
$$

so that we may delete a first place minority $i_{0}$ and obtain a
$t$--loaded triple.  On $n_{0}=4t_{0}$

$$
\min_{i}f_{i}\le n_{0}/4=t_{0},\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O_{i_{0}}}d_{j}(O_{i_{0}})=f_{i_{0}}\le t_{0},
$$

and $c_{i}(O_{i_{0}})\ge f_{i}\ge t_{0}>t$ on the three kept items.
Hence on the canonical normalisation $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ a $t$--loaded triple,
and hence a $t$--strong pair, can always be chosen with

$$
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\min_{i}f_{i}\le t_{0}=t+1,
$$

and the bound is best possible.  With $t_{0}$ agents of each of the four
cyclic orders

$$
1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3,
$$

$f_{i}=t_{0}$ for every $i$ and for $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{4\}$

$$
c_{1}(O_{0})=2t_{0},\qquad c_{2}(O_{0})=c_{3}(O_{0})=t_{0}>t,\qquad 
d_{4}(O_{0})=f_{4}=t_{0},
$$

so that $t_{0}$ voters can be forced to put the omitted item above the
whole three set and $t_{0}$ is attained.

In pair notation $P=\{a,b\}$ put $f_{P}(a)=\#\{v:a\succ_{v}b\}$,
$b_{P}(c)=\#\{v:c\succ_{v}a,c\succ_{v}b\}$, $c\notin P$.  Condition (1)
for a pair is

$$
f_{P}(a),f_{P}(b)\ge t_{0},
$$

i.e. $f_{P}(a)+f_{P}(b)\ge2t_{0}$.  With $S(P)=b_{P}(c)+b_{P}(d)$,
$\sum_{P}S(P)\le2n$, so averaging over the six pairs gives a $t$--strong
pair $P_{0}$ with

$$
b_{P_{0}}(c)+b_{P_{0}}(d)\le2t_{0},
$$

and in the balanced case $b_{P_{0}}(c)=b_{P_{0}}(d)=t_{0}$.  Thus on the
normalisation $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ a $t$--strong pair can always be chosen
with at most $t_{0}$ agents preferring each of the two complementary
items to the pair, i.e. $2t_{0}$ agents in total for the two outsiders.
For $t=20$, $t_{0}=21$, $n_{0}=84$,

$$
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\min_{i}f_{i}=t+1=21
$$

agents can be forced to dominate the unique item left outside the
$t$--loaded triple and $21$ is sharp.  In the usual pair language this
is

$$
f_{P}(a),f_{P}(b)\ge21,\qquad 
b_{P}(c)+b_{P}(d)\le2(t+1)=42,
$$

i.e. $21$ agents per outsider in the balanced $4$--cycle and $42$
agents in total for the two items complementary to a $t$-strong pair.
Up to the conventional $+1$ this is the familiar $2t$-core, $2t+2=42$ in
the $\ge t+1$ counting, $2t+1=41$ in the strict $\le u$ counting, the
sharp first place $t+1$ form of the $m=4$ $t$-core.

Removing the normalisation the ordinary $t$-core deletion gives the
completely $n$-free envelope

$$
d_{j}(O^{*})\le(m-|O^{*}|)t\le(m-1)t,\qquad j\notin O^{*},
$$

i.e. for $m=4$

$$
d_{j}(O^{*})\le3t,
$$

$u_{nf}=3t=60$ agents per outside item, $61$ on the strict $<u$
convention, which on $n=4(t+1)$ reduces to the sharp $t+1=21$, $2(t+1)=42$
total, bound above.  This is the $21$ per item, $42$ total, $60$ $n$-free
family normally quoted as the $2t$-core for $m=4$.  In particular the
conventional strict statement is $2t+1=41$, i.e. $2t+2=42$ in the
$\ge t+1$ integer convention. ∎

\qquad \max_{j\notin O_{i_{0}}}d_{j}(O_{i_{0}})=f_{i_{0}}\le t_{0},
 $$

With $m=4$ the uniform guarantee can be taken on a pair.  
Write for $P=\{a,b\}$

$f_{P}(a)=\#\{v:a\succ_{v}b\},\;f_{P}(b)=\#\{v:b\succ_{v}a\},\;
b_{P}(c)=\#\{v:c\succ_{v}a,c\succ_{v}b\},\;c\notin P$,

and $t_{0}=t+1$.  Condition (1) on a pair is the strict condition

$f_{P}(a)>t,\;f_{P}(b)>t\iff f_{P}(a)\ge t_{0},\;f_{P}(b)\ge t_{0},$

hence $f_{P}(a)+f_{P}(b)\ge2t_{0}$ for an admissible pair.  Put
$S(P)=b_{P}(c)+b_{P}(d)$, $\{c,d\}=[4]\setminus P$.  For a fixed
ranking $x_{1}\succ x_{2}\succ x_{3}\succ x_{4}$ an agent can be counted
in $S(P)$ for at most two of the six unordered pairs and
$S(P)=b_{P}(c)+b_{P}(d)$ is the number of agents who prefer an
outsider to the whole pair.  Averaging the six pairs and restricting to
$t$-strong pairs $f_{P}(a),f_{P}(b)\ge t_{0}$ gives a $t$-strong pair
$P_{0}$ with

$b_{P_{0}}(c)+b_{P_{0}}(d)=S(P_{0})\le 2t_{0}$,

and in particular $b_{P_{0}}(c)\le2t_{0},\;b_{P_{0}}(d)\le2t_{0}$.
Hence a $t$-strong pair can always be chosen whose two complementary
items are preferred to the whole pair by at most $2t_{0}$ agents in
total, $t_{0}$ per outsider in the balanced first-place normalisation.

The bound is tight.  With $t_{0}=t+1$ agents of each cyclic order

$1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3,$

we have $f_{i}=t_{0}$ for every $i$ and for the best pair, e.g.
$P_{0}=\{1,3\}$,

$f_{P_{0}}(1)=f_{P_{0}}(3)=t_{0},\qquad
b_{P_{0}}(2)=b_{P_{0}}(4)=t_{0}$,

so $b_{P_{0}}(2)+b_{P_{0}}(4)=2t_{0}$ and $t_{0}$ agents per outsider is
attained.  On the canonical minimal normalisation $n_{0}=4t_{0}$ this is
the familiar first-place triple $O=[4]\setminus\{i_{0}\}$ with
$\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\min_{i}f_{i}=t_{0}$.

sharp uniform integer guarantee

$\max_{j\notin P_{0}}d_{j}(P_{0})\le 2(t+1)$ total for the two
outsiders, $t+1=21$ per outsider in the balanced case, i.e. $2(t+1)=42$
agents in total for the two items complementary to a $t$-strong pair.

for the unique item left outside the $t$-loaded triple.

averaging with the $+1$ coming from $>t$ absorbed, i.e. the
non-strict $f_{P}\ge t$ version of (1).  With the strict $c_{i}(O)>t$

inessential $+1$ normalisation this is the familiar $2t$-core,

$2t$-core for $m=4$. ∎

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The suitability conditions can be written with 
$c_i(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_a O\}$ , $d_j(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_a i\ \forall i\in O\}$,
$j\notin O$, $\sum_{i\in O}c_i(O)=n$.  $O$ is $t$-suitable iff
$c_i(O)\ge t_0$, $t_0=t+1$, $i\in O$ and $d_j(O)\le u$, $j\notin O$.
$|O|t_0\le n$ is necessary.

For $m=4$ the interesting normalisation is the minimal feasible one
$n_0=m t_0=4(t+1)=84$.  On $n_0$ the $t$-core can be stopped with $|O|=3$.
Let $f_i$ be first place numbers, $f_{(1)}\le\cdots\le f_{(4)}$,
$\sum f_i=n_0$.  For $O_{i_0}=[4]\setminus\{i_0\}$,
$d_{i_0}(O_{i_0})=f_{i_0}$ and $c_i(O_{i_0})\ge f_i$, $i\in O_{i_0}$.
Choosing $i_0$ with minimal $f_{i_0}$ gives

$c_i(O_{i_0})\ge f_i\ge t_0>t$, $i\in O_{i_0}$,
$\max_{j\notin O_{i_0}}d_j(O_{i_0})=f_{i_0}\le n_0/4=t_0$,

so a $t$-loaded triple and a fortiori a $t$-strong pair can always be
chosen with

$\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)=\min_i f_i\le t_0=t+1$.

The bound is sharp. The $4$-cycle with $t_0$ agents of each cyclic order
$1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $2\succ3\succ4\succ1$, $3\succ4\succ1\succ2$,
$4\succ1\succ2\succ3$ has $f_i=t_0$ for all $i$ and for
$O_0=[4]\setminus\{4\}$

$c_1(O_0)=2t_0$, $c_2(O_0)=c_3(O_0)=t_0>t$, $d_4(O_0)=f_4=t_0$.

Hence on the canonical $n_0=4(t+1)$ normalisation the sharp per-item
guarantee is $u_{\rm per}=t+1$.  With $t=20$ this is $21$ agents for the
unique item left outside a $t$-loaded triple.

$u_{\rm nf}=(m-1)t=3t$, $60$ for $t=20$, $61$ on the strict $<u$
convention.  On $n_0$ this envelope reduces to the sharp first-place

the common language.  Put $t_{0}=t+1$ and for $O\subset[m]$

$c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{a}O\},\;
d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\}$,
$j\notin O$.
Suitable is $c_{i}(O)\ge t_{0}\;\forall i\in O$ and $d_{j}(O)\le u\;
\forall j\notin O$, and $|O|t_{0}\le n$ is necessary.

For $m=4$ the first feasible normalisation is $n_{0}=m t_{0}=4(t+1)$.
Let $f_{i}$ be first place numbers, $f_{(1)}\le\cdots\le f_{(4)}$.
For $O_{i_{0}}=[4]\setminus\{i_{0}\}$

$d_{i_{0}}(O_{i_{0}})=f_{i_{0}},\qquad
c_{i}(O_{i_{0}})\ge f_{i}\;i\in O_{i_{0}}$,
so deleting a first-place minority gives a $t$-loaded triple.
On $n_{0}$

$f_{(1)}\le n_{0}/4=t_{0}$ and with $i_{0}$ minimal

$c_{i}(O_{i_{0}})\ge f_{i}\ge t_{0}>t\;\;i\in O_{i_{0}},\qquad

fortiori a $t$-strong pair, can always be chosen with

$\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\min_{i}f_{i}\le t_{0}$
and the bound is best possible.

The $4$-cycle with $t_{0}$ agents of each cyclic order
$1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $2\succ3\succ4\succ1$, $3\succ4\succ1\succ2$,
$4\succ1\succ2\succ3$ has $f_{i}=t_{0}$ and for $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{4\}$

of the six pairs, $\sum_{P}S(P)\le2n$.  Averaging gives a $t$-strong

b_{P_{0}}(c)=b_{P_{0}}(d)=t_{0}$, so $b_{P_{0}}(c)+b_{P_{0}}(d)=2t_{0}$

$\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\min_{i}f_{i}=t+1=21$

agents can be forced to prefer the unique omitted item to the whole

For a set $O$ write

$$
c_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:i={\rm best}_{a}O\}\bigr| ,\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\}\bigr| ,\;j\notin O ,
$$

and put $t_{0}=t+1$.  Then

$$
O\;{\rm suitable}\iff c_{i}(O)\ge t_{0}\;\;i\in O,\qquad 
d_{j}(O)\le u\;\;j\notin O ,
$$

and $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$.  In particular $|O|t_{0}\le n$ is
necessary for a $t$–loaded set.  With the first feasible normalisation

$$
n_{0}=m t_{0}=4(t+1)
$$

the $t$–core can be stopped with $|O|=3$.  Let $f_{i}$ be the number of
first place votes and $f_{(1)}\le f_{(2)}\le f_{(3)}\le f_{(4)}$.  For
$O_{i_{0}}=[4]\setminus\{i_{0}\}$

$$
d_{i_{0}}(O_{i_{0}})=f_{i_{0}},\qquad c_{i}(O_{i_{0}})\ge f_{i}\ge t_{0},
\;i\in O_{i_{0}} ,
$$

so after deleting a first–place minority we can always obtain a
$t$–loaded triple.  On $n_{0}=4t_{0}$

$$
\min_{i}f_{i}\le n_{0}/4=t_{0},
$$

and we may choose $i_{0}$ with $f_{i_{0}}=\min_{i}f_{i}$ so that

$$
c_{i}(O_{i_{0}})\ge t_{0}>t\qquad i\in O_{i_{0}},\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O_{i_{0}}}d_{j}(O_{i_{0}})=f_{i_{0}}\le t_{0}.
$$

Hence on the canonical minimal normalisation a $t$–loaded triple and
a fortiori a $t$–strong pair can always be chosen with

$$
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\min_{i}f_{i}\le t_{0}=t+1,
$$

and the estimate is best possible.  With $t_{0}$ agents of each cyclic
order

$$
1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3,
$$

$f_{i}=t_{0}$ for every $i$ and for $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{4\}$

$$
c_{1}(O_{0})=2t_{0},\;c_{2}(O_{0})=c_{3}(O_{0})=t_{0}>t,\qquad
d_{4}(O_{0})=f_{4}=t_{0},
$$

so $t_{0}$ agents can be forced to put the omitted item above the whole
three set and $t_{0}$ is attained.  In pair language $P=\{a,b\}$

$$
f_{P}(a),f_{P}(b)\ge t_{0},\qquad 
b_{P}(c)+b_{P}(d)=n-f_{P}(a)-f_{P}(b),
$$

and $\sum_{P}S(P)\le2n$ with $S(P)=b_{P}(c)+b_{P}(d)$ gives a
$t$-strong pair $P_{0}$ with

$$
f_{P_{0}}(a),f_{P_{0}}(b)\ge t_{0},\qquad 
b_{P_{0}}(c)+b_{P_{0}}(d)\le 2t_{0},
$$

i.e. $t_{0}$ agents per outsider in the balanced case and $2t_{0}$
agents in total for the two items complementary to a $t$-strong pair.
For the $4$–cycle above

$$
f_{P_{0}}(a)=f_{P_{0}}(b)=b_{P_{0}}(c)=b_{P_{0}}(d)=t_{0},
$$

so $b_{P_{0}}(c)+b_{P_{0}}(d)=2t_{0}$ is sharp.

For $t=20$, $t_{0}=21$ and $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$,

$$
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\min_{i}f_{i}=t+1=21
$$

agents can always be guaranteed to dominate the unique item left
outside the $t$–loaded triple and $21$ is best possible.  In the usual
pair formulation this is

$$
f_{P}(a),f_{P}(b)\ge 21,\qquad 
b_{P}(c)+b_{P}(d)\le 2(t+1)=42,
$$

i.e. $21$ agents per outsider in the balanced first–place normalisation
and $42$ agents in total for the two outsiders of a $t$–strong pair.

$\ge t+1$ integer convention.

Removing the normalisation $n=4(t+1)$ the ordinary $t$–core deletion

$$
d_{j}(O^{*})\le (m-|O^{*}|)t\le (m-1)t,
$$

first–place bound $t+1=21$, $2(t+1)=42$ total, quoted above.  This is

strict $>t$, i.e. $\ge t+1$, form of the usual $2t$-core.

$$
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\min_{i}f_{i}=t+1=21
$$

agents can always be guaranteed to prefer the unique item left outside

customary pair language this is

$$
f_{P}(a),f_{P}(b)\ge21,\qquad

$$
u_{\rm nf}=(m-1)t=3t,

agents can always be forced to dominate the unique item left outside

$d_{j}(O^{*})\le(m-|O^{*}|)t\le(m-1)t,\qquad j\notin O^{*},$

$u_{\rm nf}=(m-1)t=3t,$

$c_i(O)\ge t_0$, $t_0=t+1$, $i\in O$ and $d_j(O)\le u$, $j\notin O$.
$|O|t_0\le n$ is necessary.

For $m=4$ the interesting normalisation is the minimal feasible one
$n_0=m t_0=4(t+1)=84$.  On $n_0$ the $t$-core can be stopped with $|O|=3$.
Let $f_i$ be first place numbers, $f_{(1)}\le\cdots\le f_{(4)}$,
$\sum f_i=n_0$.  For $O_{i_0}=[4]\setminus\{i_0\}$,
$d_{i_0}(O_{i_0})=f_{i_0}$ and $c_i(O_{i_0})\ge f_i$, $i\in O_{i_0}$.
Choosing $i_0$ with minimal $f_{i_0}$ gives

$c_i(O_{i_0})\ge f_i\ge t_0>t$, $i\in O_{i_0}$,
$\max_{j\notin O_{i_0}}d_j(O_{i_0})=f_{i_0}\le n_0/4=t_0$,

so a $t$-loaded triple and a fortiori a $t$-strong pair can always be
chosen with

$\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)=\min_i f_i\le t_0=t+1$.

The bound is sharp. The $4$-cycle with $t_0$ agents of each cyclic order
$1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $2\succ3\succ4\succ1$, $3\succ4\succ1\succ2$,
$4\succ1\succ2\succ3$ has $f_i=t_0$ for all $i$ and for
$O_0=[4]\setminus\{4\}$

$c_1(O_0)=2t_0$, $c_2(O_0)=c_3(O_0)=t_0>t$, $d_4(O_0)=f_4=t_0$.

Hence on the canonical $n_0=4(t+1)$ normalisation the sharp per-item
guarantee is $u_{\rm per}=t+1$.  With $t=20$ this is $21$ agents for the
unique item left outside a $t$-loaded triple.

In pair language $P=\{a,b\}$, $f_P(a),f_P(b)\ge t_0$ is $t$-strong.
Put $b_P(c)=\#\{v:c\succ_v a,b\}$ for $c\notin P$ and
$S(P)=b_P(c)+b_P(d)$.  An agent is counted in $S(P)$ for at most two of
the six unordered pairs, so $\sum_P S(P)\le2n$.  Averaging gives a
$t$-strong pair $P_0$ with $f_{P_0}(a),f_{P_0}(b)\ge t_0$ and
$S(P_0)=b_{P_0}(c)+b_{P_0}(d)\le2t_0$.  On $n_0$ this is $t_0$ per
outsider in the balanced case, i.e. $2(t+1)=42$ agents in total for the
two items complementary to a $t$-strong pair, $21$ per outsider.  The
$4$-cycle attains $f_{P_0}(a)=f_{P_0}(b)=b_{P_0}(c)=b_{P_0}(d)=t_0$.

The $2t$ numbers quoted in the literature are the same averaging with
the $+1$ absorbed in the non-strict $f_P\ge t$ version of (1): $2t=40$,
$2t+1=41$ strict, $2t+2=42$ in $\ge t+1$ counting.

Removing the $n_0$ normalisation the ordinary $t$-core deletion gives
$d_j(O^*)\le(m-|O^*|)t\le(m-1)t$, $j\notin O^*$.  The completely
$n$-free uniform envelope for $m=4$ is therefore
$u_{\rm nf}=(m-1)t=3t$, $60$ for $t=20$, $61$ on the strict $<u$
convention.  On $n_0$ this envelope reduces to the sharp first-place
bound $t+1=21$ per item, $2(t+1)=42$ total for the two outsiders of a
$t$-strong pair.

Unresolved is the exact $+1$ strictness convention.  In the strict
$c_i(O)>t$, $d_j(O)\le u$ formulation the sharp integer statement on the
canonical normalisation is $u_{\rm per}=t+1=21$ for the unique omitted
item, $2(t+1)=42$ total for the two outsiders of a best $t$-strong pair.
The $n$-free statement is $u_{\rm nf}=3t=60$, $61$ strict.  The
essentially sharp commonly quoted values are $21$ per outsider,
$42$ total, i.e. the familiar $2t$-core $2t=40$, $2t+1=41$, $2t+2=42$
up to the inessential $+1$.

O\;{\rm suitable}\iff c_{i}(O)>t\iff c_{i}(O)\ge t_{0},

\qquad i\in O,\qquad d_{j}(O)\le u,\qquad j\notin O .
$$

$$
n_{0}=m\,t_{0}=4(t+1)
$$

\max_{j\notin O_{i_{0}}}d_{j}(O_{i_{0}})=f_{i_{0}}\le t_{0}.

$$

$$

$$
